These are not abstract virtues. They are becoming the signals that more capable agent evaluation will learn to weight. Building for that horizon rather than gaming the current state is the recommendation, not a certainty about outcomes, but the bet with the better long-term structure. Attribution also varies. A system may cite a source, summarize it without a useful route back, or produce an answer without retrieving that page at all. Being available to the system is therefore a different outcome from receiving traffic or revenue. The economic return needs to be tested separately. Reach logic: what you optimized for Maximize impressions across surfaces Hook in the first three seconds Frequency and engagement drive distribution Volume compounds audience Success: eyes on content Indexing logic: what compounds from here Be in the reference set for your domain Depth and verifiable specificity over hook Consistency of perspective over time Credibility that survives agent evaluation Success: cited or synthesized when it counts Keep the archive usable: stable links, clear dates, named authors, primary sources, and corrections readers can find. These help people inspect the work and can make retrieval easier. They do not guarantee that an assistant will select the work or that selection will support the business. Indexing today favors incumbents. The strategic argument is about the direction of travel as evaluation systems mature. Build for the horizon, not the current state. The synthesis-not-citation problem: you can be indexed and invisible. The economic model for that position is still forming. Build the asset now, monetize when the model clarifies. Section III / Four Three Models That Survive The three models below are proposals to test. An established archive or direct audience may give a publisher a starting advantage, but neither determines the outcome. A newer publication can start with a narrower domain and examine whether the work produces repeat attention and a viable return. The models assume that some people will respond to delegated routine consumption by seeking more deliberate engagement. Others may spend the time elsewhere. Do not assume the size of either group. Look at repeat reading, replies, subscriptions, and attendance in your audience, then ask what those people value enough to support. Media organizations face an existential version of the Impression Gap: if the human eye isn't present at reception, the advertising surface disappears. For brands, the problem is more ambiguous. An agent that executes a purchase decision the human has already made or delegated is not necessarily a loss. The three models below are survival architecture for media; for brands, Model I is primary and Models II and III are supplementary. Model I Authority of Reference Predates advertising as: specialist publishing, expert reference, domain media Being the source agents surface and audiences seek for genuine interpretation of a domain. Advertising rents access to attention. Authority of reference builds a position in the judgment architecture of both agents and the humans they serve, on a different time scale, toward a different kind of durability. Why it compounds: Consistent perspective plus domain specificity plus time produces source reputation that is slow to build and expensive to replicate. The economic model (licensing, subscriptions, inbound authority) is still forming for AI contexts. Building the archive may help, but the revenue path remains unresolved and should be tested. Caveat: benefits incumbents disproportionately. Being synthesized rather than cited means the revenue mechanism is unresolved. The kill criterion for this model is about the asset, not the revenue. See the kill criteria below. Model II Direct Human Access Predates advertising as: subscriptions, events, community, direct correspondence Spaces where agent mediation is incomplete or structurally excluded. A distinction matters: newsletters and digital communities are partially mediatable: an agent can summarize a newsletter for you. Physical events, real-time interaction with verified identity, communities requiring genuine mutual recognition: structurally resistant to full substitution. What to test: People who seek out an event, publication, or community may value the direct experience enough to pay for it. Ask what they value and test an offer with them. A price increase is a hypothesis about that audience, not an automatic result of more routine consumption moving to agents. Caveat: distinguish partially-mediatable (newsletters, forums) from non-delegable (live, physical, real-time verified). The business model implications are different; the former competes with agent summarization, the latter does not. Model III Consequential Voice Predates advertising as: named editorial authority, accountability under risk, brand reputation with stakes The organization or individual that publishes under real identity, takes positions, and has something to lose when wrong. The differentiator is asymmetry: when being wrong costs something visible, being right means something real. That asymmetry is what audiences pay for when the alternative is infinite content with no author who has anything at stake. What readers can examine: Who makes the editorial decisions, how challenges are handled, and what changes after an error. These practices can apply to human and AI-assisted work. Their value depends on whether the source’s operators actually take responsibility and whether readers use that record. Horizon risk: as AI personas become more persistent and simulated accountability more convincing, the line will blur for some audiences. Specificity and verifiable track record are the defense. Kill Criteria: for people making decisions, not evaluating theses 3 signals Asset not compounding after 12 months Signal: your domain-specific body of work has not grown in depth, specificity, or consistency over a 12-month period. Measure this concretely: the number of pieces that take a falsifiable position, the percentage that cite primary sources or original data, the frequency of publication under your name in a single domain. Threshold: if those three numbers are flat or declining, you are producing content volume without building an indexing asset. Action: do not diagnose this as a distribution or monetization problem. It is an asset problem. Narrow the domain further, increase the specificity of each piece, and hold the publication frequency for 90 days before reassessing. Revenue from authority of reference is a downstream question; the asset has to exist first. Direct access stagnant vs. reach If owned and direct channels (newsletter subscribers, community members, event attendees) are not growing as a share of total audience over 12 months, even as distributed reach holds or grows, you are not converting presence into access. Reach maintained, direct access stagnant is the specific failure mode to act on, not the aggregate number. Deliberate minority contracting If behavioral signals of deliberate engagement (completion rates, response rates, direct conversion, attendance) are declining as a share of total audience interactions, the fraction of your audience that will benefit from the three models is contracting. This is the earliest warning that your domain is moving toward passive consumption. It does not mean abandon the strategy. It means the pricing, positioning, and community structure need adjustment before the gap becomes unbridgeable. For media: existential. For brands: a positioning challenge for agent-era purchase criteria. The models are the same; the urgency is not. Pricing: deliberate human attention is repricing upward now, before the scarcity is legible to everyone. The window is open. Not indefinitely. Kill criterion #1 is about the asset, not the revenue. Build the archive. The conversion path will clarify when the indexing model matures. Section IV / Four The Position This paper is for media builders, brand strategists, and editorial directors: anyone whose economic model is directly attached to what happens in the space between something published and the human who receives it. The Impression Gap closes that space in a growing number of contexts. The three models are the structures that survive and strengthen as it does. Two types of claims have been made throughout. Some are empirical: the Gap is real, measurable in specific domains now, expanding in a consistent direction. Others are strategic recommendations: building authority of reference, direct human access, and consequential voice now positions you advantageously for the transition as it matures. The first can be observed and verified. The second depends on your domain, your starting position, and how quickly the transition reaches your specific context. The map is accurate in direction. The distance is yours to measure. The series that follows takes each consequence of the Impression Gap into its specific domain: what happens to engagement when presence is automated, to brand identity when representation is delegated, to content strategy when there are two filters before a human reader, to the trust architecture when the implicit contract of online presence expires without ceremony, and to what you build today so that you have genuine gravity when the transition makes these questions urgent for everyone. The work starts with a small test in your own audience. Establish which encounters involve people, what those people return for, and whether a proposed offer serves them. Use that evidence to decide which of these models, if any, deserves a larger investment. Empirical: the Gap is real and expanding. Strategic: building for it now positions you for the transition. The first is verifiable. The second is a bet with structure behind it. You were always building for human attention. The Impression Gap removes the proxy. What's left is the thing that was always worth building for. After You Post / Reading Path Five essays on the social fabric of the agent internet 01 The Empty Room On engagement as a measure of human presence, and what it measures when most of the presence is automated. 02 The Proxy Self On identity and delegation: what it means for your brand presence to become a training dataset rather than a living signal. 03 Writing for the Filter On content that has to pass two algorithmic layers before reaching a human, and why that changes what good editorial strategy is. 04 The Trust Collapse On the implicit contract of online presence, and what happens to audience trust when it breaks without ceremony. 05 Origin Gravity On what survives when the intermediated web becomes agent territory, and how to build it before you need it. If the impression gap concerns you, The Transition Tax names the five structural costs of living through this shift.

the-last-manual-moment.html.before: I built Chango on a Tuesday night. Chango is an autonomous agent running on a Raspberry Pi in my home. Small device, the size of a deck of cards, sitting on a shelf doing things I tell it to do without me being in the room. I spent a few nights putting it together, adjusting its personality, watching it respond, adjusting again. At some point it started doing what I intended it to do and I sat back and felt something I didn't have a word for immediately. It wasn't pride exactly. It wasn't excitement in the way launching a product feels exciting. It was something closer to vertigo. The kind you get when you look down from somewhere higher than you expected to be. What surprised me wasn't what Chango did. It was the sudden, total clarity about what everything that comes after Chango is going to be. More autonomous. More capable. More present in the decisions that used to belong exclusively to humans. The specific thing Chango did that night was almost beside the point. What landed was the irreversibility of the moment. The sense that I had crossed something. That the world I was sitting in on that Tuesday night was the last version of the world where this was still unusual. That feeling has a name. I've been calling it the last manual moment. The point just before something that required human effort, human judgment, human time, stops requiring those things. We pass through these moments constantly now. Most of them go unmarked. We notice the capability when it arrives and forget to notice what it replaced. What happens to the habit of working through a question when an answer is always available? That is what I keep coming back to when I think about Lucas growing up with these tools. ◆ This is not a new observation. Every generation has lived through a transition that restructured what it meant to be useful. The printing press made the memorized text less valuable. The calculator made mental arithmetic less impressive. The photograph made the hand-painted portrait into a different kind of object entirely, not worse, just no longer the only way to fix a face in time. Each time, something that had been scarce became abundant, and the humans who had organized their sense of worth around that scarce thing had to find another place to stand. What's different now is the scope. Previous transitions automated specific capabilities. This one is reaching toward general intelligence. Not perfectly, not completely, not without limits that matter. But in the direction of general. The gap between what a capable AI system can do and what a capable human can do is closing faster in more domains than any previous technology managed. And unlike the calculator, which made arithmetic abundant while leaving reasoning intact, this transition is arriving at reasoning itself. You could always tell a child who worried about calculators: learn to think, not just to calculate. The thinking was safe. The refuge was clear. What do you tell a child today, when the refuge itself is becoming less exclusive? My son Lucas is twelve. He uses AI for his homework already, or he will soon, the way his generation uses everything: without ceremony, without the weight of novelty, because it was simply there when he arrived. He doesn't know what the internet felt like before recommendation algorithms. He doesn't know what research felt like before search. He will not know what thinking felt like before AI assistance, because he will never have had to think without it available. I'm not sure that's a tragedy. I'm not sure it isn't. ◆ What I keep returning to is a specific kind of loss that I can't quite argue is a loss. The friction of not knowing. The experience of sitting with a question that had no immediate answer, of having to hold uncertainty long enough to develop a real relationship with it, of reaching a conclusion slowly and therefore owning it in a way that a fast answer doesn't produce. There is something that happens in a human mind when it struggles with a hard problem over time. The struggle is not inefficiency. It is the process by which understanding becomes durable rather than temporary. When you fight to understand something, when you fail and try again and fail differently and eventually arrive somewhere, you carry the map of that journey inside you. You know not just the answer but the shape of the problem. You know where the traps are because you fell into them. AI gives you the answer. It does not give you the journey. And for most purposes, in most moments, the answer is what you needed. But there is a category of human capability that only develops through the journey, through the sustained struggle, through the experience of being genuinely lost and finding your way back. I don't know what happens to that category when the journey becomes optional. I don't think anyone does yet. Lucas is going to grow up with Chango on the shelf. With systems far more capable than Chango available in his pocket, in his classroom, in every professional context he enters. He will be more capable in certain measurable ways than any generation before him. He will be able to produce, to synthesize, to analyze, to create at a scale that would have seemed impossible when I was his age. What I don't know is whether he will develop the specific kind of depth that only comes from doing things the hard way, from not having the answer available, from sitting alone with a problem until the problem changes you. That's the thing I can't prepare him for. Not because I don't want to. Because the world that required that depth in order to survive is the world that's ending. And the world that comes after it hasn't decided yet what it values. ◆ Here is what I think survives. Not as a list of skills for the future economy. As a conviction about what is human in ways that can't be replicated. The first is consequence. The willingness to be wrong in ways that cost something real. AI systems are extraordinarily capable of producing recommendations, analysis, and synthesis. They bear zero cost when they are wrong. They have no reputation that degrades with bad calls, no relationships that break when the advice fails, no career that ends when the strategy collapses. A human who puts their name on something, who is publicly committed to a position, who has skin in the game, carries a kind of authority that doesn't come from capability. It comes from risk. That doesn't disappear when intelligence becomes abundant. It becomes more valuable precisely because the abundance makes it rarer. The second is genuine surprise. The capacity to encounter something you didn't know you needed and let it change you. AI systems optimizing for stated preference are extraordinarily good at giving you what you asked for. My concern is whether systems built around our stated preferences leave enough room for encounters we did not plan. The encounter with the genuinely unexpected: the book you didn't choose, the conversation that took you somewhere you didn't plan to go, the problem that turned out to be a different problem entirely. That is where human minds develop in ways that preference satisfaction cannot produce. Protecting the conditions for genuine surprise, in your own life and in the lives of the people you're raising, is not nostalgia. It is maintenance of the capacity that makes everything else meaningful. The third is physical presence. Not as sentiment but as mechanism. The things that can only happen when people are in the same room: a shared meal, a long silence, a crisis navigated together in real time. These are not going to be replicated by any system. They are going to become more precious as more of life migrates to mediated interaction. And they are going to become the only proof available that something happened between humans, not just through them. In a world where most interaction can be delegated, the choice to be present becomes the signal itself. ◆ I can't prepare Lucas for the world he's going to inherit. That world doesn't fully exist yet and the parts that do are changing faster than any preparation I could offer. What I was taught about how to build a career, how to develop expertise, how to make yourself valuable: some of that will apply to him and some of it will be worse than useless because it will point him toward the wrong things with real confidence. What I can do is something smaller and more durable. I can model what it looks like to keep building in conditions of genuine uncertainty. To make things that matter, slowly, with your name on them. To be wrong sometimes and say so. To stay curious about the things that are hard to understand rather than delegating the understanding. To treat the people in the room as the primary thing rather than the documentation of having been in the room. I built Chango. I think Chango is remarkable. I think what Chango represents, the autonomous, tireless, infinitely scalable intelligence that is going to restructure everything, is one of the most significant developments in human history. I'm glad to be alive at this moment to see it. And I still think the most important thing I can do for my son is show him what a human being looks like when they take their work seriously. With the weight that comes from knowing it matters whether you do it well or poorly, whether you show up or don't, whether you tell the truth or find a way around it. ✦ ❧ ✦ That is what I want to teach Lucas as this changes. It's a lesson about what being a person means when the world keeps changing underneath you. It's the only lesson I actually know how to give. Essay · Diego Dell'Agostino

the-last-scarcity.html.before: Essay · March 2026 The LastScarcity Published March 7, 2026 · Updated September 14, 2026 · by Diego Dell'Agostino A late-night bot project led me to ask what gives work its pull when the immediate problem has been solved. Diego Dell'Agostino · Buenos Aires DESIRE PRODUCTION EVERYTHING EXCEPT THIS Document Map 7 Sections I Setup Five dominoes, four down II Argument The thing behind the thing III Trap The dignity trap IV Market The desire economy V Break The thing that almost killed this essay VI Turn I am the problem VII Close No map for this Last Monday I made fifty dollars in two minutes. I was with people from work, after hours, and a coworker had Polymarket open on his laptop. For those who don't know it: Polymarket is a prediction market. People bet on whether things will happen. Elections, interest rates, crypto prices. It is gambling dressed in a blazer. Watching him operate was a Pandora's box moment. He wasn't doing anything sophisticated. He was just reading the lines, seeing where they looked wrong, and placing small bets. Bitcoin up or down in the next five minutes. And it was working. And the thought arrived immediately, the way obvious thoughts do, fully formed and impossible to un-think: if he can do this, why can't I? I placed a bet. Bitcoin, up or down, next five minutes. The line looked wrong to me. Not wrong in a sophisticated quantitative-finance way. Wrong in the way a crooked painting looks wrong. You don't measure the angle. You just see it. Two minutes later: fifty dollars. I closed the app. Now, fifty dollars is a nice dinner. It is not a revelation. If this story were about the fifty dollars, I would not be writing it and you would not be reading it. This story is about what happened when I got home. The offer was real. So was what it revealed. Both can be true at the same time. Because here's the thing about my brain, and maybe yours: it doesn't care about the fifty dollars. It cares about the crack. The inefficiency. The fact that a line on a screen was wrong and I could see it. And I'd already been working with autonomous AI agents for months, bots that do things on their own, around the clock, while you sleep. So the fifty dollars wasn't a payday. It was a proof of concept. And I didn't want to make money. I wanted to prove a point. I went home. Made steak sandwiches and a salad for dinner. Ate with my son and my wife. Didn't do the dishes because according to her I do them wrong, and she's probably right. Normal Monday night. But the whole time, while I was cutting bread and wiping the counter and going through the motions of a regular evening, the thought was turning in the back of my head like a rock tumbler. If he can do this, why can't I? And if I can do this, why can't a bot? By 11 PM the house was quiet. I walked to my desk. Opened a terminal. And started building. I built a small bot to repeat the process with one-dollar bets and a position-sizing rule based on the Kelly criterion. Keeping the stakes small was part of the experiment. It did not make the bot immune to losses, bad estimates, or execution errors. By midnight I had a prototype. By 1 AM I was testing it against historical data and seeing gains in the simulation. That was enough to keep me working, though it did not establish what would happen with real trades. By 1:45 AM I was in the kitchen pouring a coffee, thinking about what I had just built. The thought was: if a 43-year-old media guy from Buenos Aires with no trading background can make fifty dollars in two minutes because he watched a coworker do it first, and if a bot can scale that 24/7 while he sleeps, and if that bot can be copied infinitely, then what is work? What is it for? And if the answer isn't money anymore, is there an answer at all? The coffee got cold. I didn't drink it. I went back to my desk. Not to work on the bot. The bot was done. I went back to sit with the question. And it's been sitting with me since. I Section I / Seven Five dominoes, four down Scarcities feel permanent. Like gravity. Like weather. Like a rule so old nobody remembers who wrote it. But they're not rules. They're dominoes. And they've been falling for ten thousand years. We just don't notice because each one takes a few centuries to land. Domino one: food. For most of human history, almost all human effort went into not dying of hunger. The agricultural revolution tipped this one over. Slowly, brutally, unevenly. But it fell. Today, and I want you to sit with this, more humans die from eating too much than from eating too little. If you told that to a farmer in 1200 AD, he would think you were describing heaven. Or a mental illness. Domino two: information. Wanted to know something in 1950? Library. If your town had one. If it had the book. If the book was in your language. If you could afford the time to go. Knowledge was locked behind geography, money, and institutions. The internet blew the door off. And then the problem flipped. We went from "I can't find anything" to "I can't stop finding things." The scarcity of information was replaced by the scarcity of attention. We solved one hunger and invented another. Domino three: production. This one is falling right now, and you can hear the wood cracking. AI doesn't help you make things. AI makes things. Code, images, music, legal briefs, product designs, medical diagnoses, marketing strategy. One person with the right tools now produces what a team of twenty did five years ago. The marginal cost of producing almost anything is on a trajectory that ends at a number very close to zero. My bot, the one I built between 11 PM and 1 AM on a Monday while my kid slept, will probably never make me rich. But it will make money while I do nothing. Domino four: capital. This is the one I felt that Monday night. When autonomous agents can find and exploit inefficiencies across markets, around the clock, without salary or ego or sleep, the ability to generate returns disconnects from human effort. You don't need to be smart. You don't need to work hard. You don't even need to be awake. You need an agent and a Wi-Fi password. And if I can build that in two hours, what can a real team build in two months? Four dominoes. Four scarcities that organized all of human civilization. All either fallen or falling. There's a fifth one still standing. It is the question I want to focus on here: what gives people a reason to act? II Section II / Seven The thing behind the thing Solving the practical problem did not settle what I wanted to do next. When you're starving, food is the meaning of life. You don't need purpose. You need bread. The need for bread gives you a structure, a direction, a reason to wake up. It's awful. It's also clear. Now: get the bread. Solve the hunger. Watch what happens. You don't feel fulfilled. You feel a new emptiness, one that was always there but the hunger was covering it up, the way loud music covers a crack in the wall. Turn off the music and the crack is suddenly the only thing in the room. There was a French psychoanalyst named Jacques Lacan who figured this out sixty years ago. He had a term for it that sounds ridiculous in English, objet petit a, the "little object a", but the idea behind it might be the most important idea for understanding the next century. Lacan's idea: you never actually want the thing you think you want. You want the wanting. The thing you're chasing, the job, the raise, the apartment, the person, the fifty dollars, that thing is just a stand-in for a deeper pull that has no object. Desire isn't aimed at anything. It's aimed at the gap between where you are and where you aren't yet. Close the gap and you don't feel satisfied. You feel empty. Because the gap was the engine. And you just turned it off. Think about the last thing you really wanted. Remember the wanting? The planning, the energy, the obsession? Now remember the moment you got it. Was the getting as good as the wanting? It almost never is. That's not a bug. That's how desire works. The getting was never the point. The movement was the point. And this has massive, terrifying consequences for a world that is about to solve every material scarcity on the list. If each solved scarcity reveals the one underneath, and if material scarcities were covering up an existential one, then we are about to experience, at global scale, for the first time in the history of the species, a world where nothing is scarce except the reason to get out of bed. The European aristocracies already ran a small version of this experiment. They had food, shelter, capital, security, and unlimited time. Same resources across the board. The results were, and this is the word I want you to hold, bimodal. Some of them made extraordinary things. Art that outlasted empires. Science that rewired our understanding of the universe. Philosophy we're still teaching. Others destroyed themselves. Gambling halls, opium, duels over nothing, a slow gorgeous rot. Same resources. Opposite outcomes. The difference wasn't intelligence. Wasn't education. Wasn't money. The difference was whether they had a because. A pull. A crack they couldn't stop looking at. I use leisure in earlier societies as an imperfect comparison. Those arrangements depended on exclusion and other people’s labor. They cannot tell us what would happen if more people had time they did not need to sell. They do make me want to ask how someone learns to use that time. III Section III / Seven The dignity trap El trabajo dignifica. Work dignifies. My grandfather said it. The politician says it. The motivational poster in the break room says it. It sounds so obviously true that nobody ever checks. If work dignifies, then every sweatshop is a cathedral. Every data-entry clerk is glowing with purpose. Every person grinding a job they hate, in a building they resent, for a boss who doesn't know their name, to pay rent on an apartment they're never awake in long enough to enjoy. That person should feel dignified. They don't. They feel used. They feel like the hours of their one life are being converted into someone else's profit at an exchange rate they didn't set and can't negotiate. That's not dignity. That's a transaction with bad terms and no exit clause. So what is dignity? I'll tell you what it felt like at 1 AM on that Monday. It felt like choosing. Choosing to build something nobody asked for because my brain wouldn't let it go. Choosing to stay up because the problem was more interesting than sleep. The choice was the dignity. Not the work. The agency. The fact that I could have stopped and I didn't stop because I didn't want to stop. Your value as a human, proportional to your output. Produce nothing, be nothing. That's the operating system AI is about to crash. "Work dignifies" equates effort with virtue and rest with sin. And it's been the operating system of capitalism for three hundred years: your value as a human is proportional to your output. Produce more, be worth more. Produce nothing, be nothing. AI is about to crash that operating system. Not gently. Because when a machine produces more than you, faster, cheaper, better, without complaint or vacation or existential crises, and when your value was always defined by output, then by the logic of the system that raised you: you are worth nothing. That's not a policy problem. That's an identity crisis on a civilizational scale. And the proposed solution, the one you hear in every policy paper and conference talk, is UBI. Universal Basic Income. Give everyone money. Floor established. Problem solved. UBI solves the stomach. It does not solve the 6 AM ceiling stare. The 6 AM ceiling stare. That's the real problem. What do you do when you wake up and nothing requires you? Your bills are paid. Your fridge is full. Your bot is making money. And you're lying there, in the dark, and the question lands on your chest like a brick: now what? UBI is necessary. A floor is necessary. Nobody should starve while we figure this out. But UBI is the first sentence of an answer. And the answer is a book. A book nobody has written. A book I'm not sure we know how to write. But I think I know what Chapter 2 looks like. IV Section IV / Seven The desire economy If the old economy ran on production, and production is being automated, what does the next economy run on? I think the answer is desire. Not desire the way marketers use it: countdown timers, manufactured urgency designed to bypass your prefrontal cortex. Desire the way Lacan used it: the force that moves a person toward something they can't quite reach, and in the reaching, they find out who they are. I think this also changes what people may be willing to pay for. When I got home that Monday and sat down to build the bot, the old economy had nothing to do with it. Nobody was paying me. Nobody assigned it. There was no KPI, no deadline, no performance review. I didn't even want the money. I wanted to prove that it could be done. A crack in a system that my brain could not leave alone. That pull is desire in its purest economic form. I produced something valuable, a working autonomous trading agent, not because of incentive structure. Because of a point I needed to make, mostly to myself. The old economy captured labor: give me your time, I'll give you money. The new economy will need to capture desire: give me a reason to move, and I'll give you everything I have for free and stay up until 2 AM doing it. Audiences watch. Congregations belong. In a world of infinite free content, watching is worth zero. Belonging is priceless. Some of this is already visible, if you know where to look. Audiences are dying. Congregations are being born. An audience watches. A congregation belongs. In a world where AI generates infinite free content, watching has a market value of approximately zero. Belonging is priceless. People already pay fifty dollars a month for private Discord servers when every piece of information ever produced is available for free. What are they buying? Not content. They're buying a border. An inside and an outside. A room small enough to feel real. Some people choose limits when a service offers more than they want to consume: a finite camera roll, an app blocker, a quieter phone. I am interested in limits that help someone keep a commitment they chose. That is different from claiming all scarcity has become optional, or that restricted access automatically creates desire. And the entrepreneur of the future doesn't make products. She makes contexts. Reasons to move. Polymarket didn't invent betting. Betting is ancient. Polymarket created a context where betting is civic participation, prediction, intellectual sport. The mechanism is old. The meaning is new. That's the business model: not what you build, but what reason to move you give people. But there's a hole in this whole theory. A big one. And it almost killed the essay, because for three days I couldn't figure out what was bothering me about my own argument. Then I did. V Section V / Seven The thing that almost killed this essay Here's what was bothering me. I'd been writing about desire, about cracks, about the importance of gaps and mystery and the not-knowing. And then I looked at the dominant ideology of the industry I work in and realized it wants the exact opposite: total transparency. Open source. Open data. Open protocols. Blockchain's entire pitch is radical legibility: every transaction visible, every process auditable, every shadow eliminated. The tech industry has spent twenty years building toward a world of total light. No hidden corners. No asymmetry. No fog. The dream is a planet-sized clean room where nothing is unclear and everything is optimized. Beautiful idea. Terrible, terrible outcome. My fifty dollars on Polymarket existed because of a shadow. An inefficiency. A crack where the price didn't match reality. If the market were perfectly transparent and perfectly efficient, that crack wouldn't exist. The price would already be right. There'd be nothing to see, nothing to bet on, nothing to build a bot for. And I'd still be scrolling. Desire needs exactly the thing transparency destroys: a veil. A perfectly lit room has no depth. A perfectly efficient market has no game. A perfectly transparent world has no reason to explore it. This isn't an argument against transparency in governance, in justice, in institutions. That's non-negotiable. But total transparency as a universal principle? As a dogma applied to every market, every interaction, every system? That kills the thing that makes humans go. The shadow. The not-knowing. The suspicion that something is hidden and worth finding. So the next economy doesn't just need to produce desire. It needs to protect it. To deliberately preserve zones of opacity and productive inefficiency. Spaces where the answer isn't visible. Because the not-knowing is the pull. And the pull is all that's left. That's the hole in the theory, and it's also the answer. The desire economy isn't just about creating reasons to move. It's about protecting the conditions that make movement possible. Including, and this is the hard part, the right to not see everything. The right to a shadow. VI Section VI / Seven I am the problem I need to tell you who you've been listening to. I'm 43. I live in Buenos Aires. I have a twelve-year-old son who beats me at chess and doesn't know it yet, but he sure does know that he can beat me at Rocket League and Super Smash Brothers, and he does. Oh boy he does. I grew up copying cassettes from the radio and I've spent my whole adult life bouncing between media and technology, never quite fitting in either. I co-founded Argentina's first podcast production company. I had a blog for years where I wrote about whatever a young guy entering adulthood writes about when he doesn't know what he's doing yet. I'm not a writer, or at least I've never called myself one. I'm the guy who keeps seeing cracks in things and can't leave them alone. And a few years ago I saw what AI could do to broadcast and content and I threw myself into it headfirst. Now I run AI-powered broadcast systems for a Bitcoin media company. I'm not a programmer. I'm not an engineer. I'm someone who adopted AI so aggressively that it became the centerpiece of everything I do. I didn't build the machine. I moved in. The speed of iteration still catches me off guard. I can try something in an evening that I would previously have needed help to prototype. Some attempts stop there; others become tools I keep using. My hands can now get ahead of my judgment about which ideas deserve another night. I am, in a very literal sense, the person who saw what AI could do to media production and said yes, more, faster, replace everything that can be replaced. I am an active participant in the demolition of the economy this essay says we need to replace. Not as the engineer who built the engine. As the guy who saw the engine, understood what it meant, and reorganized his entire life around it. I don't know if that's better or worse. I am the problem. And I can't stop. Not because of the money. I could make money other ways. I can't stop because the wiring is the crack. Figuring out how to connect the tools, how to make the systems talk, how to turn a pile of AI capabilities into something that works at 3 AM without a human. That's the pull. The 2 AM compulsion to make the system work is the exact desire I've been theorizing about for six sections from a comfortable analytical distance that I no longer deserve. So here it is, the confession without the clean vantage point: I'm warning you about the flood from the deck of a boat I'm selling. The contradiction is real and it's mine and I cannot resolve it. The bot runs. The broadcast systems ship. The content generates while I sleep. And I sit here writing about the death of work while actively accelerating it. If you find that disqualifying, I understand. If you find it clarifying, I think you're right. That is my contradiction: I build tools that reduce the work needed to do something, then stay up late because building them is the work I want to do. I do not know how widely that feeling will travel. I know it is present at my desk. And this is where my son enters the essay for the last time. He is twelve. If he grows up in a world where earning a living requires less work, what will give his days direction? That is a scenario I want to think through with him, not a future I can promise him. It's "what do I do with my life?" He will still need to learn how to make a living. I also want him to have practice choosing work when the reason for doing it is curiosity, care, or a commitment he has made to someone. Those questions deserve time alongside preparation for a job. The Greeks had a word for what he'll need. Skholē. The free activity of a citizen who doesn't have to work for survival and therefore can dedicate himself to what actually matters. Not because someone pays him. Because it pulls him. The catch: Greek skholē was for citizens. Slaves did the work. The fields didn't farm themselves. But now the slaves are agents. Bots. Algorithms. The fields are farming themselves. And the question that sounds naive is the one that won't leave me alone: do we go back to the classical? Do we actually return to the original condition, the one where basic needs are covered and what's left is the human project? Painting, thinking, building, arguing, making something that didn't need to exist but does because someone couldn't not make it? Is this the circle closing after ten thousand years? Maybe. But the circle doesn't close evenly. And that's the part that keeps me up. VII Section VII / Seven No map for this I want to be honest about something. I don't know how this ends. But I can see how it splits. Because here's what the desire economy does if you're not careful: it widens the gap. Not the income gap. The agency gap. The gap between people who know what to do with freedom and people who drown in it. The aristocrats showed us this already. Same resources, opposite outcomes. Now scale that to eight billion. The people who can reason, who can direct the tools, who know what to ask for, they'll live in skholē. The people who can't will live in a subsidized paralysis that looks like comfort and feels like nothing. AI can make it easier to produce an answer before you have worked out whether it is sound. The value still depends on how you frame the task, check the result, and revise it. That is why I keep coming back to education: people need practice with those decisions as well as access to the tool. The gap that's opening is not between those who have AI and those who don't. It's between those who can think and those who delegated the thinking before they learned how. That's the real danger of the transition. Not unemployment. Not robots. Not superintelligence. The danger is a world where the tools are free, the access is universal, the floor is guaranteed, and the thing that determines whether you build a cathedral or stare at the ceiling is something no policy can distribute: the capacity to want something specific and pursue it with the full weight of your attention. We are entering territory without precedent. And I don't mean "unprecedented" the way people use it to describe a bad quarter or an unusual election. I mean: there is no prior. No case study. No analogue. "This is like the Industrial Revolution." It's not. The Industrial Revolution replaced muscle; the mind was still necessary. "This is like the printing press." It's not. The printing press still needed someone with something to say. There is no playbook for this because this has never happened. The question has changed. For ten thousand years the question was: how do we produce enough? That question organized everything. Agriculture, industry, capitalism, globalization, the internet, AI. All of it was a different answer to "how do we make more?" The answer worked so well that it made itself obsolete. We figured out how to produce enough. Now we're standing in a room full of everything we asked for, looking at each other, wondering why the room feels empty. The 21st century doesn't have a production problem. It has a desire problem. How do we desire well? Not want. Not consume. Desire. How do we maintain the pull, the midnight itch, the crack that won't let you sleep, the need to build the thing nobody asked for, in a world that is systematically removing every external reason to move? How do we protect the gap that makes us go? Policy and technology can change the conditions in which someone chooses. They do not choose a particular project for them. I keep coming back to my own desk at 2 AM: what am I still reaching for when the task that brought me here is already done? And yet you are. ✦ ❧ ✦ I finished the Polymarket bot. It works. You can't give it to someone with a policy or a paycheck or a subscription. It can only come from inside a body that wants something it can't quite name. the-last-scarcity.html.after: The Last Scarcity A late-night bot project led me to ask what gives work its pull when the immediate problem has been solved. Published March 7, 2026 · Updated September 14, 2026 · by Diego Dell'Agostino Document Map 7 Sections I Setup Five dominoes, four down II Argument The thing behind the thing III Trap The dignity trap IV Market The desire economy V Break The thing that almost killed this essay VI Turn I am the problem VII Close No map for this Last Monday I made fifty dollars in two minutes. DESIRE PRODUCTION EVERYTHING EXCEPT THIS I was with people from work, after hours, and a coworker had Polymarket open on his laptop. For those who don't know it: Polymarket is a prediction market. People bet on whether things will happen. Elections, interest rates, crypto prices. It is gambling dressed in a blazer. Watching him operate was a Pandora's box moment. He wasn't doing anything sophisticated. He was just reading the lines, seeing where they looked wrong, and placing small bets. Bitcoin up or down in the next five minutes. And it was working. And the thought arrived immediately, the way obvious thoughts do, fully formed and impossible to un-think: if he can do this, why can't I? I placed a bet. Bitcoin, up or down, next five minutes. The line looked wrong to me. Not wrong in a sophisticated quantitative-finance way. Wrong in the way a crooked painting looks wrong. You don't measure the angle. You just see it. Two minutes later: fifty dollars. I closed the app. What stayed with me was the question I took home: could I build a system to test what I thought I had seen? The offer was real. So was what it revealed. Both can be true at the same time. I had been experimenting with agents for months. This gave me another problem to try. One winning bet did not establish an edge, but it was enough to send me back to the desk. I went home. Made steak sandwiches and a salad for dinner. Ate with my son and my wife. Didn't do the dishes because according to her I do them wrong, and she's probably right. Normal Monday night. But the whole time, while I was cutting bread and wiping the counter and going through the motions of a regular evening, the thought was turning in the back of my head like a rock tumbler. If he can do this, why can't I? And if I can do this, why can't a bot? By 11 PM the house was quiet. I walked to my desk. Opened a terminal. And started building. I built a small bot to repeat the process with one-dollar bets and a position-sizing rule based on the Kelly criterion. Keeping the stakes small was part of the experiment. It did not make the bot immune to losses, bad estimates, or execution errors. By midnight I had a prototype. By 1 AM I was testing it against historical data and seeing gains in the simulation. That was enough to keep me working, though it did not establish what would happen with real trades. By 1:45 AM I was in the kitchen pouring a coffee, thinking about what I had just built. The thought was: if a 43-year-old media guy from Buenos Aires with no trading background can make fifty dollars in two minutes because he watched a coworker do it first, and if a bot can scale that 24/7 while he sleeps, and if that bot can be copied infinitely, then what is work? What is it for? And if the answer isn't money anymore, is there an answer at all? The coffee got cold. I didn't drink it. I went back to my desk. Not to work on the bot. The bot was done. I went back to sit with the question. And it's been sitting with me since. I Section I / Seven Five dominoes, four down Different technologies have changed what takes time, effort, and money. I use four examples to get to the question that kept me at the desk. They involve different limits; none shows that basic needs have been solved for everyone. Food. Producing food and making it available to the people who need it are different problems. My thought experiment begins with material security; it does not claim that everyone has it. Domino two: information. Wanted to know something in 1950? Library. If your town had one. If it had the book. If the book was in your language. If you could afford the time to go. Knowledge was locked behind geography, money, and institutions. The internet blew the door off. And then the problem flipped. We went from "I can't find anything" to "I can't stop finding things." The scarcity of information was replaced by the scarcity of attention. We solved one hunger and invented another. Production. AI lets me prototype some tools much faster than before. That changes what I can attempt in an evening. It does not remove the work of deciding whether the result is reliable or worth maintaining. My bot, the one I built between 11 PM and 1 AM on a Monday while my kid slept, will probably never make me rich. But it will make money while I do nothing. Capital. The bot made me wonder how much market work could be delegated. My experiment could not answer that. A system that places trades still risks capital, and a short run tells me little about its performance over time. These changes made me think about the work I would choose if fewer hours were needed to meet immediate demands. They do not establish that material scarcity is ending. There's a fifth one still standing. It is the question I want to focus on here: what gives people a reason to act? II Section II / Seven The thing behind the thing Solving the practical problem did not settle what I wanted to do next. When you're starving, food is the meaning of life. You don't need purpose. You need bread. The need for bread gives you a structure, a direction, a reason to wake up. It's awful. It's also clear. Now: get the bread. Solve the hunger. Watch what happens. You don't feel fulfilled. You feel a new emptiness, one that was always there but the hunger was covering it up, the way loud music covers a crack in the wall. Turn off the music and the crack is suddenly the only thing in the room. There was a French psychoanalyst named Jacques Lacan who figured this out sixty years ago. He had a term for it that sounds ridiculous in English, objet petit a, the "little object a", but the idea behind it might be the most important idea for understanding the next century. Lacan's idea: you never actually want the thing you think you want. You want the wanting. The thing you're chasing, the job, the raise, the apartment, the person, the fifty dollars, that thing is just a stand-in for a deeper pull that has no object. Desire isn't aimed at anything. It's aimed at the gap between where you are and where you aren't yet. Close the gap and you don't feel satisfied. You feel empty. Because the gap was the engine. And you just turned it off. Think about the last thing you really wanted. Remember the wanting? The planning, the energy, the obsession? Now remember the moment you got it. Was the getting as good as the wanting? It almost never is. Getting something I wanted has sometimes left me looking for another problem. I recognize that pattern at my desk; I cannot turn it into a rule about everyone’s desires. Suppose a person has more time they do not need to sell. What helps them choose how to use it? That is the scenario I want to examine, rather than assume technology delivers it to everyone. The European aristocracies already ran a small version of this experiment. They had food, shelter, capital, security, and unlimited time. Same resources across the board. The results were, and this is the word I want you to hold, bimodal. Some of them made extraordinary things. Art that outlasted empires. Science that rewired our understanding of the universe. Philosophy we're still teaching. Others destroyed themselves. Gambling halls, opium, duels over nothing, a slow gorgeous rot. I use leisure in earlier societies as an imperfect comparison. Those arrangements depended on exclusion and other people’s labor. They cannot tell us what would happen if more people had time they did not need to sell. They do make me want to ask how someone learns to use that time. III Section III / Seven The dignity trap El trabajo dignifica. Work dignifies. My grandfather said it. The politician says it. The motivational poster in the break room says it. It sounds so obviously true that nobody ever checks. If work dignifies, then every sweatshop is a cathedral. Every data-entry clerk is glowing with purpose. Every person grinding a job they hate, in a building they resent, for a boss who doesn't know their name, to pay rent on an apartment they're never awake in long enough to enjoy. That person should feel dignified. They don't. They feel used. They feel like the hours of their one life are being converted into someone else's profit at an exchange rate they didn't set and can't negotiate. That's not dignity. That's a transaction with bad terms and no exit clause. So what is dignity? I'll tell you what it felt like at 1 AM on that Monday. It felt like choosing. Choosing to build something nobody asked for because my brain wouldn't let it go. Choosing to stay up because the problem was more interesting than sleep. The choice was the dignity. Not the work. That's the operating system AI is about to crash. "Work dignifies" equates effort with virtue and rest with sin. And it's been the operating system of capitalism for three hundred years: your value as a human is proportional to your output. Produce more, be worth more. Produce nothing, be nothing. Desire the way Lacan used it: the force that moves a person toward something they can't quite reach, and in the reaching, they find out who they are. I think this also changes what people may be willing to pay for. When I got home that Monday and sat down to build the bot, the old economy had nothing to do with it. Nobody was paying me. Nobody assigned it. There was no KPI, no deadline, no performance review. I didn't even want the money. I wanted to prove that it could be done. A crack in a system that my brain could not leave alone. That pull is desire in its purest economic form. I produced something valuable, a working autonomous trading agent, not because of incentive structure. Because of a point I needed to make, mostly to myself. A project can draw effort that no one commissioned. I want to understand what makes that effort worthwhile to the person doing it. Audiences watch. Congregations belong. In a world of infinite free content, watching is worth zero. Belonging is priceless. A paid community may offer a place to participate, receive attention, and build relationships. Those reasons to join differ from access to information. A product needs to discover which of them its members actually value. Some people choose limits when a service offers more than they want to consume: a finite camera roll, an app blocker, a quieter phone. I am interested in limits that help someone keep a commitment they chose. That is different from claiming all scarcity has become optional, or that restricted access automatically creates desire. That gives me a product question: what are people choosing to take part in, beyond the task the tool completes? The answer needs to come from their experience, not from my explanation of it. The argument also leaves me with a tension: I value transparent systems, yet the uncertainty of an unsolved problem is often what draws me to work on it. V Section V / Seven The thing that almost killed this essay Open source. Open data. Open protocols. Blockchain's entire pitch is radical legibility: every transaction visible, every process auditable, every shadow eliminated. The tech industry has spent twenty years building toward a world of total light. No hidden corners. No asymmetry. No fog. The dream is a planet-sized clean room where nothing is unclear and everything is optimized. My fifty dollars on Polymarket existed because of a shadow. An inefficiency. A crack where the price didn't match reality. If the market were perfectly transparent and perfectly efficient, that crack wouldn't exist. The price would already be right. There'd be nothing to see, nothing to bet on, nothing to build a bot for. And I'd still be scrolling. Desire needs exactly the thing transparency destroys: a veil. A perfectly lit room has no depth. A perfectly efficient market has no game. A perfectly transparent world has no reason to explore it. This isn't an argument against transparency in governance, in justice, in institutions. That's non-negotiable. But total transparency as a universal principle? As a dogma applied to every market, every interaction, every system? That kills the thing that makes humans go. The shadow. The not-knowing. The suspicion that something is hidden and worth finding. So the next economy doesn't just need to produce desire. It needs to protect it. To deliberately preserve zones of opacity and productive inefficiency. Spaces where the answer isn't visible. Because the not-knowing is the pull. And the pull is all that's left. I want room to explore questions whose answers I do not have. That does not require hiding information from the people affected by a system. VI Section VI / Seven I am the problem I'm 43. I live in Buenos Aires. I have a twelve-year-old son who beats me at chess and doesn't know it yet, but he sure does know that he can beat me at Rocket League and Super Smash Brothers, and he does. Oh boy he does. I grew up copying cassettes from the radio and I've spent my whole adult life bouncing between media and technology, never quite fitting in either. I co-founded Argentina's first podcast production company. I had a blog for years where I wrote about whatever a young guy entering adulthood writes about when he doesn't know what he's doing yet. I'm not a writer, or at least I've never called myself one. I'm the guy who keeps seeing cracks in things and can't leave them alone. And a few years ago I saw what AI could do to broadcast and content and I threw myself into it headfirst. Now I run AI-powered broadcast systems for a Bitcoin media company. I'm not a programmer. I'm not an engineer. I'm someone who adopted AI so aggressively that it became the centerpiece of everything I do. I didn't build the machine. I moved in. The speed of iteration still catches me off guard. I can try something in an evening that I would previously have needed help to prototype. Some attempts stop there; others become tools I keep using. My hands can now get ahead of my judgment about which ideas deserve another night. I am, in a very literal sense, the person who saw what AI could do to media production and said yes, more, faster, replace everything that can be replaced. I am an active participant in the demolition of the economy this essay says we need to replace. Not as the engineer who built the engine. As the guy who saw the engine, understood what it meant, and reorganized his entire life around it. I don't know if that's better or worse. I am the problem. And I can't stop. Not because of the money. I could make money other ways. I can't stop because the wiring is the crack. Figuring out how to connect the tools, how to make the systems talk, how to turn a pile of AI capabilities into something that works at 3 AM without a human. That's the pull. The 2 AM compulsion to make the system work is the exact desire I've been theorizing about for six sections from a comfortable analytical distance that I no longer deserve. That is my contradiction: I build tools that reduce the work needed to do something, then stay up late because building them is the work I want to do. I do not know how widely that feeling will travel. I know it is present at my desk. He is twelve. If he grows up in a world where earning a living requires less work, what will give his days direction? That is a scenario I want to think through with him, not a future I can promise him. It's "what do I do with my life?" He will still need to learn how to make a living. I also want him to have practice choosing work when the reason for doing it is curiosity, care, or a commitment he has made to someone. Those questions deserve time alongside preparation for a job. The Greeks had a word for what he'll need. Skholē. The free activity of a citizen who doesn't have to work for survival and therefore can dedicate himself to what actually matters. Not because someone pays him. Because it pulls him. The catch: Greek skholē was for citizens. Slaves did the work. The fields didn't farm themselves. Automation raises a different question from that historical arrangement: could it give more people time for work they choose? That depends on who owns the tools, who receives the gains, and which work still has to be done. Maybe. But the circle doesn't close evenly. And that's the part that keeps me up. Access to tools and time would not give everyone the same preparation or choices. That is why I want the discussion to include education and support, rather than divide people into those who can use freedom and those who cannot. AI can make it easier to produce an answer before you have worked out whether it is sound. The value still depends on how you frame the task, check the result, and revise it. the-proxy-self.html.before: After You Post · 02 · March 2026 The ProxySelf Published March 10, 2026 · Updated September 14, 2026 · by Diego Dell'Agostino A public profile can keep repeating a position after its author has moved on. What happens to the relationship? Diego Dell'Agostino · Buenos Aires PERSON PROXY SEVERED same name, two selves The previous essay asked whether the room you're publishing into still has people in it. This one asks a harder version of the same question: whether you, as the person publishing, are still the one in the room. There's a creator you've probably followed for a couple of years. Consistent voice, consistent cadence, consistent point of view. Something happened to them in the last eighteen months, you're not sure what, a shift in tone maybe, or a subject they used to care about going quiet. But the posting didn't stop. The content kept coming. The presence held. You noticed but didn't think much of it. People change. Algorithms change. Maybe they found a new angle. You kept following. One possible explanation is that more of the account’s activity has been delegated. Section 01 The Split That Was Always There There's always been a gap between who you are and what you publish. That's not a problem specific to the internet. Every writer knows it, every public figure knows it: the version of you that goes out into the world is edited, curated, timed. The full person stays home. For most of the social web's history, that gap was small enough to ignore. You published more or less what you thought, at more or less the pace you thought it, and the result read like you. Rough around the edges, occasionally off, but recognizably yours. The presence and the person were close enough that conflating them felt harmless. That started changing in two directions at once, and neither of them felt like a decision at the time. Optimization came first. The longer you published, the more you learned what worked: what the algorithm rewarded, what the audience responded to, which framings got shared and which ones disappeared. Slowly, without deciding to, you started writing toward the signal. Not lying, not performing, just leaning. The presence began to diverge from the person in ways too gradual to notice. Then came delegation. Scheduling tools, then drafting tools, then agents that could approximate a voice. The presence started running on its own. Both paths end up in the same place: a version of you that keeps going when you're not there. Section 02 Severance Called It Something Else The show Severance built a whole architecture around this. An employee undergoes a procedure that splits their consciousness: the version that goes to work (the innie) has no memory of life outside the office. The version that lives outside (the outie) has no idea what happens during the workday. Same body, same name, two people who will never meet. What makes it unbearable isn't the split itself. It's that the innie works in the name of someone they don't know. The outie lives a life the innie will never see. And everything the innie produces goes out into the world attributed to a whole person who is actually two halves with no shared memory. The innie is your agent, your scheduled content, your optimized presence: consistent, trained on what works, producing on schedule, with no access to what's actually happening in your life. The outie is you: living, changing, having a bad month, quietly losing interest in the thing the agent is still passionate about on LinkedIn. What the system knows about you is almost entirely innie. The outie is the part that doesn't post. Until the two share a feed. The birthday post goes up between two pieces of scheduled content and nobody flags the transition. The algorithm doesn't see a different person. It sees the same profile, the same handle, more data points to process. That's where the signal degrades. The optimized content picks up a trace of the human moment by adjacency. The human moment gets catalogued as more output from the same profile that produces everything else. Both lose definition. And over time, the model learns the pattern of your unoptimized moments well enough to start incorporating them into its picture of you. The outie, just by showing up, is teaching the innie how to sound like it. In Severance the two worlds never touch by design. In your feed they touch every day, without ceremony, without anyone noticing. And the split doesn't require an agent. You don't have to have delegated anything intentionally. The agent self emerges from the optimization alone, from years of learning what your audience responds to and adjusting accordingly. If you've been publishing consistently for long enough, there's already a version of your presence that operates on its own logic. Delegation just makes the separation visible. Section 03 What the System Reads What gets scraped, indexed, and used to train models is the agent. The person doesn't have a corpus. The person exists in conversations, in the things you didn't publish, in the ideas you had and then dropped. None of that makes it into the dataset. A language model that knows your work is developing a picture of the agent. A potential client researching you is reading the agent. Part of your professional reputation is now a searchable record that keeps existing regardless of whether you still hold those positions or still speak in that register. There's a version of you that keeps publishing after you've moved on. Not because anyone is lying. Because the presence developed enough momentum to continue on its own terms. This was always true to some degree. A published essay from 2019 doesn't update when you change your mind. But the velocity is different now, and the gap between the living person and the indexed presence can open faster than anyone thinks to close it. Section 04 What the Agent Leaves Behind A birthday post, a weekend photo, or an offhand observation can matter because of the experience a reader associates with the person. Those posts can also be scheduled or assisted. The personal subject alone does not reveal how they were produced. But as the agent takes up more of the presence, the baseline shifts. What used to read as human variation starts to read as noise against a smoother signal. The birthday post becomes an anomaly in your own feed instead of a human moment in it. And every consistent presence is, quietly, a training set. Years of public output add up to a record of how you think: what you frame as problems, what you treat as obvious, what you find worth saying at all. Enough of it and a model can predict what you'd say about something you've never addressed. The question is whose voice that model is learning. The person you are now, or the version the algorithm built while you were teaching it what worked. ✦ ❧ ✦ The presence persists. The person keeps moving. At some point those two things are worth comparing. diegodella.ar · Buenos Aires, 2026 Share After You Post · Reading Path 01 The Empty Room 02 The Proxy Self 03 Writing for the Filter 04 The Trust Collapse 05 Origin Gravity The Empty Room Writing for the Filter

The algorithm doesn't see a different person. It sees the same profile, the same handle, more data points to process. That's where the signal degrades. The optimized content picks up a trace of the human moment by adjacency. The human moment gets catalogued as more output from the same profile that produces everything else. Both lose definition. And over time, the model learns the pattern of your unoptimized moments well enough to start incorporating them into its picture of you. The outie, just by showing up, is teaching the innie how to sound like it. In Severance the two worlds never touch by design. In your feed they touch every day, without ceremony, without anyone noticing. And the split doesn't require an agent. You don't have to have delegated anything intentionally. The agent self emerges from the optimization alone, from years of learning what your audience responds to and adjusting accordingly. If you've been publishing consistently for long enough, there's already a version of your presence that operates on its own logic. Delegation just makes the separation visible. Section 03 What the System Reads What gets scraped, indexed, and used to train models is the agent. The person doesn't have a corpus. Part of your professional reputation is now a searchable record that keeps existing regardless of whether you still hold those positions or still speak in that register. There's a version of you that keeps publishing after you've moved on. Not because anyone is lying. Because the presence developed enough momentum to continue on its own terms.
