unfinished-arguments.html.before: Laboratory / Forward-Looking Unfinished Arguments Published February 22, 2026 · Updated September 14, 2026 · by Diego Dell'Agostino ? ? ? 7 OPEN AI and what it breaks Not predictions. Not finished frameworks. Questions that keep returning. The papers on this site argue about the present. This section argues about what comes next, and what AI is going to break when it arrives in full. Not in the general sense that everyone already agrees on. In the specific, structural sense: the exact mechanisms by which AI reshapes things we thought we understood. How trust is built. How authority is earned. How markets find things. How culture renews itself. How we know when advice is actually good. Most AI commentary operates at one of two altitudes: the very high ("everything will change") or the very low ("here is what this specific tool does"). What is missing is the middle register, the structural argument about second and third order consequences for the systems and institutions that organize human life. These are the questions at that altitude. They are not finished. Some will be wrong. All of them feel more important than the conversation happening at the other two altitudes. These are working questions. I will revise them as evidence or experience changes the argument. What this is not "AI will change everything" is not an argument. These are the specific mechanisms, named before they are proven, which is the only way to test them against reality as it arrives. The register Not tools. Not use cases. The structural logic of systems being restructured. What changes when the assumption underlying an entire field turns out to be wrong. Status Hot: direction clear, architecture forming Warm: question is right, answer not yet Open: named, unresolved, kept here to not lose it 1 Hot When the Customer Is Not the Decision-Maker AI agents buy things. What does marketing do now? Every persuasion architecture built over the last hundred years assumes a human at the moment of decision. The billboard, the landing page, the brand story, the emotional hook, the social proof: all of it operates on human psychology at the exact moment a person considers whether to act. That assumption is dissolving. AI agents are beginning to execute purchasing decisions on behalf of humans who set criteria in advance and may never review the individual choice. What does persuasion look like when the entity being persuaded has no emotions, carries no brand memories from childhood, and evaluates entirely against structured verifiable signals? The answer is not better SEO. It is a fundamentally different theory of why any organization deserves to be chosen, one built on verifiability rather than feeling, on track record rather than story, on machine-readable signals rather than human-felt associations. The criteria a person gives an assistant may reflect earlier encounters with products and sources. That gives me a question for brand work: when and how were those criteria formed, and what would cause the person to revise them? The extent of that influence needs to be observed in actual decisions. What breaks Every brand investment made on the assumption that the buyer experiences the brand at the moment of purchase. Category leadership built on emotional resonance rather than verifiable differentiation. The entire apparatus of advertising designed to intercept attention at decision time, when there is no human attention left to intercept. Horizon 18–30 months Marketing logic Brand building Agentic purchasing Signal to watch First major brand reporting that conversion from agent-mediated discovery differs systematically from human-browsing conversion in ways that cannot be explained by audience differences. Connects to Impression Gap Agent Capture 2 Hot The Death of Taste as Signal When AI produces anything on demand, what does preference reveal? Taste has always functioned as a signal of human interiority. What you prefer reveals something about who you are. Curators, editors, and critics derived authority precisely because their preferences were informative: hard to fake at scale and expensive to develop over time. A system responding to stated preferences can narrow what a person encounters, but it can also offer unfamiliar examples or recommendations. My concern is what the particular system optimizes for. Does it help someone explore beyond a familiar pattern, or keep giving them variations of what previously held their attention? That is a design and measurement question, not an incapacity built into the definition of AI. The argument forming: AI-mediated content discovery will produce a generation of people whose stated preferences become progressively more predictable, more self-referential, and less capable of genuine surprise. Not the death of culture. The calcification of individual preference into an ever-narrowing loop that feels increasingly satisfying and is actually increasingly shallow. What breaks The function of editors and curators as taste-developers rather than taste-satisfiers. The market for genuinely challenging work that does not optimize against existing preference. The mechanism by which culture renews itself through encounters people did not choose and could not have predicted they needed. Horizon 3–7 years Culture Curation Preference formation The uncomfortable version Giving people exactly what they want, at scale and with perfect efficiency, may be one of the most culturally destructive things that can be done to them. Most AI companies are not equipped to take that claim seriously. Connects to Curation Premium Constitutive Arc 3 Hot Memory and the Limits of Familiarity A system can retain context. What obligations should come with that continuity? Human trust is built through accumulated experience over time. You trust a doctor because you have seen them be right before. You trust a brand because it has consistently delivered. You trust a friend because you share a history that gives both of you a stake in the relationship continuing. Trust is, at its core, a function of memory: the record of past interactions that makes future behavior predictable. Some AI products retain information across interactions. For example, ChatGPT supports saved memories and reference to chat history , depending on settings and availability. Retained context can create continuity, but it does not by itself establish the obligations of a reciprocal relationship. The question is what a user can reasonably expect the service and its operator to remember, protect, and take responsibility for. The institutional question is who carries the relationship when AI mediates a service. A bank or advisory service may have an extensive record of a customer even if a particular model call does not. Users need to know what information is retained, where continuity breaks, and which person or organization can respond when the system gets something wrong. What breaks The assumption that familiarity and trust are the same thing. The institutions that have substituted AI efficiency for human relationship without understanding what the relationship was actually doing. And the people who mistake the feeling of being understood for actually being understood, which may be the defining psychological confusion of the next decade. Horizon 2–5 years Trust architecture Institutions Human-AI relation The deepest version If trust requires memory and AI systems are memoryless by design, widespread AI deployment in trust-dependent contexts is not just an efficiency story. It is a structural change to the substrate on which social cohesion is built. Connects to Sovereignty Debt Consequential Voice 4 Warm The Collapse of Effort as Proof When anyone can produce anything instantly, what does quality signal? Before AI, the quality of a produced thing carried implicit information about the effort behind it. A well-written essay suggested careful thought. A polished design suggested developed skill. A comprehensive research report suggested significant time invested. Quality was, among other things, a proxy for investment, and investment was a signal of commitment, care, and competence. AI breaks this proxy completely. High production quality no longer implies high investment of human time or skill. The essay, the design, the report: all of it can be produced in minutes by someone with zero relevant expertise. The signal that quality carried has been decoupled from the thing quality was signaling. The result is not just that evaluating work becomes harder. It is that the entire framework through which humans have assessed credibility based on observable output needs to be rebuilt from scratch. What replaces effort as proof? The forming hypothesis: consequence replaces effort. What someone is willing to put their name on when they could hide behind generation. What someone will defend when challenged. What someone has a visible stake in being right about. Consequentiality, not quality of output but cost of being wrong, becomes the credibility signal that effort used to provide. That is a profound restructuring of how authority is earned in almost every domain. What breaks Every evaluation system that uses quality of output as a proxy for human competence: job hiring, academic assessment, investment due diligence, deciding who to listen to. The infrastructure of credentialing, which exists to certify that the person behind the output earned the right to produce it. And the social contract that effort deserves recognition, when effort is no longer distinguishable from its absence. Horizon Now - 3 years Credibility Authority Evaluation systems Already breaking Academic institutions. Hiring processes that rely on writing samples. Peer review in research. Any process that uses quality of a produced artifact to infer something about the human behind it. Connects to Consequential Voice Occlusion Bias 5 Warm Intelligence Without Skin in the Game Who is responsible when automated advice is wrong? Nassim Taleb's argument about skin in the game is essentially about asymmetry: advice from someone who bears no cost of being wrong is structurally corrupted, regardless of the intelligence of the advisor. The doctor who recommends surgery but does not perform it. The consultant who recommends restructuring but does not manage the team through it. The advisor who recommends the investment but does not hold the position. In each case the intelligence may be genuine, the advice technically correct, and yet something is missing that no amount of better analysis compensates for. A model does not bear personal stakes in its advice. The organization providing or deploying it can still bear responsibility and reputational consequences. The practical question is whether those obligations are clear to the user and whether there is a usable process for correcting or contesting a result. As AI becomes the default advisor in more consequential domains, the absence of skin in the game stops being abstract and becomes a practical problem with measurable consequences. Not because the AI is malicious. Because consequentiality is what calibrates advice-giving over time. Without it, even excellent intelligence drifts in ways that are invisible until the cost accumulates into something that cannot be ignored. What breaks The assumption that intelligence plus information is sufficient for good advice. The institutional structures that used professional accountability as the mechanism for aligning advisor and advisee: those structures were not arbitrary, they were solving the skin-in-the-game problem that AI reintroduces at scale. And potentially: the collective ability to distinguish between advice that is analytically correct and advice that is actually actionable for the specific person receiving it. Horizon 3–6 years Decision-making Accountability AI advice The hardest version Accountability is already part of governance work such as NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework . What remains open here is how providers and operators put it into practice: who reviews disputed advice, what evidence is preserved, and what recourse the person affected can actually use? Connects to Sovereignty Debt Consequential Voice 6 Open The New Scarcity If AI can produce almost anything, what becomes expensive? Economics is the study of scarcity. When something becomes abundant it loses value. When something becomes scarce it gains it. AI is making previously scarce things abundant at extraordinary speed: writing, code, images, translation, analysis, synthesis, customer service, legal drafts, medical explanations. The economic value of those things is falling and will continue to fall. That part is not controversial. What is genuinely open: what becomes newly scarce as a result? Scarcity does not disappear. It migrates. The printing press made handwritten manuscripts obsolete and made literacy newly valuable. Photography made painted portraiture obsolete and made the commissioned portrait newly precious as a signal of status. Every technology that makes something abundant creates new scarcity somewhere else. What is the analogue for AI? I am considering deliberate human attention, visible responsibility for errors, physical presence, and opportunities to work through uncertainty. Each deserves a separate argument. Their value will depend on how people use the systems and organize the services around them, not on a definition that makes AI incapable of contributing. Why this stays open The list of new scarcities is still forming. The economic mechanisms that will price them are not yet visible. And the answer is probably domain-specific in ways that make any general claim misleading. This is the argument that needs the most time before it becomes a paper, and the one whose answer matters most for every strategic decision being made right now. Horizon 5–10 years Economics Value theory Long-term The question underneath Every strategic bet about what to build over the next decade depends on a view about what AI makes scarce. Most people are making those bets without having made that view explicit. Connects to Last Human Impression Origin Gravity 7 Hot The Tastemaker Premium When AI satisfies preference at scale, the person who can surprise you becomes unreasonably powerful Argument 2 on this page describes the death of taste as signal. This argument runs in the opposite direction and both possibilities are worth examining together. That tension is the point. When AI produces infinite content calibrated to stated preference, it creates two populations. The majority get what they asked for, efficiently and continuously. Their preference loop closes. They are satisfied in a way that makes them progressively less capable of being surprised and progressively less interested in trying. That population is large, growing, and economically important to AI companies building for scale. Some people may seek a curator because they want something outside their familiar preferences. A record of useful, unexpected selections could make that relationship valuable. It remains to be seen how that value compares with recommendations from systems designed to encourage exploration. The historical parallel is the concert after the phonograph. Before recorded music, all music was live and undifferentiated. After, recorded music became the commodity and the live performance became a categorically distinct experience with its own economy, its own pricing logic, its own meaning. The artist did not disappear. The artist became something different and more expensive precisely because mechanical reproduction created an abundance that live presence could never be part of. AI does the same thing to curation that the phonograph did to performance. The tastemaker does not compete with the abundance. They become the proof that the abundance is not enough. What this creates A stratification of cultural authority sharper than anything that existed before. The tastemakers who survive the transition, those with genuine perspective, verifiable track record, and the specific kind of authority that comes from having been right before the consensus, will hold more power over the fraction of the population that still wants to be surprised than the most followed curator in history ever held over their audience. Because the contrast with the alternative has never been this stark, and contrast is what makes scarcity legible. Horizon Now - 5 years Curation Cultural authority Scarcity The implication Would people pay more for a curator whose choices regularly help them discover something worthwhile? That is the business question I want to test, alongside whether the relationship lasts once recommendation systems improve. Connects to Authority of Reference Curation Premium Constitutive Arc These arguments are published in their current state of incompleteness. That incompleteness is the point. A finished argument that turned out to be wrong is less useful than an unfinished one asking the right question. If something here collides with something you are working on, the contact is on the about page .

A model does not bear personal stakes in its advice. The organization providing or deploying it can still bear responsibility and reputational consequences. The practical question is whether those obligations are clear to the user and whether there is a usable process for correcting or contesting a result. As AI becomes the default advisor in more consequential domains, the absence of skin in the game stops being abstract and becomes a practical problem with measurable consequences. Not because the AI is malicious. Because consequentiality is what calibrates advice-giving over time. Without it, even excellent intelligence drifts in ways that are invisible until the cost accumulates into something that cannot be ignored. What breaks The assumption that intelligence plus information is sufficient for good advice. The institutional structures that used professional accountability as the mechanism for aligning advisor and advisee: those structures were not arbitrary, they were solving the skin-in-the-game problem that AI reintroduces at scale. And potentially: the collective ability to distinguish between advice that is analytically correct and advice that is actually actionable for the specific person receiving it. Horizon 3–6 years Decision-making Accountability AI advice The hardest version Accountability is already part of governance work such as NIST’s AI Risk Management Framework . What remains open here is how providers and operators put it into practice: who reviews disputed advice, what evidence is preserved, and what recourse the person affected can actually use? Connects to Sovereignty Debt Consequential Voice 6 Open The New Scarcity If AI can produce almost anything, what becomes expensive? Economics is the study of scarcity. When something becomes abundant it loses value. When something becomes scarce it gains it. AI is making previously scarce things abundant at extraordinary speed: writing, code, images, translation, analysis, synthesis, customer service, legal drafts, medical explanations. The economic value of those things is falling and will continue to fall. That part is not controversial. What is genuinely open: what becomes newly scarce as a result? Scarcity does not disappear. It migrates. The printing press made handwritten manuscripts obsolete and made literacy newly valuable. Photography made painted portraiture obsolete and made the commissioned portrait newly precious as a signal of status. Every technology that makes something abundant creates new scarcity somewhere else. What is the analogue for AI? I am considering deliberate human attention, visible responsibility for errors, physical presence, and opportunities to work through uncertainty. Each deserves a separate argument. Their value will depend on how people use the systems and organize the services around them, not on a definition that makes AI incapable of contributing. Why this stays open The list of new scarcities is still forming. The economic mechanisms that will price them are not yet visible. And the answer is probably domain-specific in ways that make any general claim misleading. This is the argument that needs the most time before it becomes a paper, and the one whose answer matters most for every strategic decision being made right now. Horizon 5–10 years Economics Value theory Long-term The question underneath Every strategic bet about what to build over the next decade depends on a view about what AI makes scarce. Most people are making those bets without having made that view explicit. Connects to Last Human Impression Origin Gravity 7 Hot The Tastemaker Premium When AI satisfies preference at scale, the person who can surprise you becomes unreasonably powerful Argument 2 on this page describes the death of taste as signal. This argument runs in the opposite direction and both possibilities are worth examining together. That tension is the point. When AI produces infinite content calibrated to stated preference, it creates two populations. The majority get what they asked for, efficiently and continuously. Their preference loop closes. They are satisfied in a way that makes them progressively less capable of being surprised and progressively less interested in trying. That population is large, growing, and economically important to AI companies building for scale. Some people may seek a curator because they want something outside their familiar preferences. A record of useful, unexpected selections could make that relationship valuable. It remains to be seen how that value compares with recommendations from systems designed to encourage exploration. The historical parallel is the concert after the phonograph. Before recorded music, all music was live and undifferentiated. After, recorded music became the commodity and the live performance became a categorically distinct experience with its own economy, its own pricing logic, its own meaning. The artist did not disappear. The artist became something different and more expensive precisely because mechanical reproduction created an abundance that live presence could never be part of. AI does the same thing to curation that the phonograph did to performance. The tastemaker does not compete with the abundance. They become the proof that the abundance is not enough. What this creates A stratification of cultural authority sharper than anything that existed before. The tastemakers who survive the transition, those with genuine perspective, verifiable track record, and the specific kind of authority that comes from having been right before the consensus, will hold more power over the fraction of the population that still wants to be surprised than the most followed curator in history ever held over their audience. Because the contrast with the alternative has never been this stark, and contrast is what makes scarcity legible. Horizon Now - 5 years Curation Cultural authority Scarcity The implication Would people pay more for a curator whose choices regularly help them discover something worthwhile? That is the business question I want to test, alongside whether the relationship lasts once recommendation systems improve. Connects to Authority of Reference Curation Premium Constitutive Arc If one of these questions connects with something you are building, send me the example . A case that contradicts the argument would be useful.

work-posta.html.before: Posta · Case study Building a podcast company before podcasting became obvious. Posta started in Buenos Aires in 2014. The work was to build more than a catalog: a product, a production system, marketing and distribution, audience and community relationships, a commercial model, and enough shared language for people and brands to understand a format that was still early. The context. Podcasting had already proved that on-demand audio could produce new voices and formats. In Latin America, though, it was not yet an obvious category for listeners, advertisers, or media companies. There was no established playbook to import intact. Posta had to make work people wanted to hear while helping create the market around the work. The problem. How do you turn an emerging format into a durable media company before distribution, audience habits, production conventions, and brand demand have settled? Editorial Make shows worth returning to Original formats needed a recognizable point of view, reliable production, and a catalog rather than isolated experiments. Product Treat the company as a media product Programming, packaging, listening behavior, distribution, and audience feedback had to inform one another. Audience and community Create reasons to return, participate, and share Reach mattered, but so did repeat listening, direct feedback, recognizable formats, and relationships that could outlast a single release. Business Build demand around an unfamiliar format Branded audio and partnerships required translating podcasting into something organizations could understand and use without flattening the medium. Operations Make creative work repeatable Production, publishing, marketing, and client work needed workflows that could scale beyond the founders doing everything. My role. I co-founded Posta and worked across product, marketing, growth, positioning, and business development. Early company building rarely respects department boundaries. The useful job is often translating between the editorial idea, the audience behavior, the commercial opportunity, and the system the team can actually operate. The company built original programming, branded audio, distribution relationships, and work across multiple Latin American markets. Those outcomes belonged to a larger team and to my co-founders; this page describes the parts of the system I know from direct involvement. What changed. Posta moved from an early format bet to an established Spanish-language podcast company. In December 2022, PodX acquired a majority stake in Posta, its first investment in Latin America. The company remains part of the PodX studio group. Public evidence: PodX's studio directory , the acquisition announcement , and LA NACION's 2022 report . What Posta taught me about AI-native media. Distribution The business changes before the format feels settled Podcasting was not only radio delivered through a different file. On-demand distribution changed programming, measurement, packaging, and the relationship between a show and its audience. Economics Lower production costs change what gets to exist When a format becomes cheaper to make and distribute, more specific ideas become viable. AI will do this again, but cheaper output alone does not create a useful media product. Discovery Interfaces matter as much as content A strong show can remain invisible if the surrounding product cannot help the right listener find, understand, and return to it. Operations Workflows outlast tools Tools change quickly. A clear editorial standard, production sequence, ownership model, and recovery path are more durable. That is why I use AI-native media to mean a change in the operating system, not a layer of generated content added to an old one. Continue. Next case Building a 24/7 global media operation From a new format to a continuous, distributed production system. Current territory AI-Native Media How AI changes workflows, interfaces, production, discovery, and distribution. Identity About Diego Background, current work, and authoritative external profiles.

work.html.before: Work Selected things I've helped build, scale, or operate. Two cases that show how media, product, marketing, content, audience relationships, and operations have to work together when a format or company is still taking shape. Posta Podcast company · Buenos Aires and Latin America Posta began in 2014, before podcasting was an obvious media category in the region. The work was not only making shows. It was building the product, explaining the format to audiences and brands, developing repeat listening and community relationships, creating repeatable production and distribution, and turning an editorial idea into an operating company. Context A format before its market On-demand audio had promise, but limited shared language, established commercial models, or regional production infrastructure. Role Co-founder Product, marketing, growth, positioning, and business development across the company's development. What changed From experiment to regional company Posta built an original catalog, branded audio work, and operations beyond Argentina. PodX acquired a majority stake in 2022. Read the Posta case study Roxom TV 24/7 global live media · San Francisco, London, Hong Kong Roxom TV posed a different problem: how to run a live global media product continuously without copying the cost structure and organizational shape of a traditional television network. Context Continuous output across time zones Live production, editorial work, real-time data, programming, and recovery paths had to behave like one system. Role Founding team Media architecture and product operations, including workflows, internal tools, automation, and remote operational work. What changed A distributed operating model Studios across three continents connected to shared product, editorial, production, and AI-assisted workflows. Read the Roxom TV case study The thread between them. Posta and Roxom TV look like different kinds of media company. The underlying work was similar: connect product, marketing, content, audience, and operations so a shift in distribution or production becomes a system people can run every day. That foundation now runs through my work on AI-native media : how research, interfaces, workflows, editorial operations, distribution, communities, and decision-making change when AI becomes part of the infrastructure. For more examples of what I am building, see the public product shelf . For the ideas behind the work, start with Writing . Bring a concrete problem. A new format, a production workflow that keeps breaking, or a product people struggle to understand: these are useful starting points. I look at the audience, the editorial decisions, the tools, and who has to run the work every day. Tell me what you are building, what is getting stuck, and what needs to change. The cases above show the kind of work I bring to that conversation. Discuss a project

writing-for-the-filter.html.before: After You Post · 03 · March 2026 Writing forthe Filter Published March 10, 2026 · Updated September 14, 2026 · by Diego Dell'Agostino On content that has to pass two algorithmic layers before reaching a human, and why that changes what good editorial strategy is. Diego Dell'Agostino · Buenos Aires FILTER 01 FILTER 02 TWO MACHINES before the human There used to be one machine between you and a human reader. You learned to write for it. That was the job. Now there are two. The first decides whether to surface your content. The second, sitting between the first and the actual person, decides whether to read it. They have different criteria. The second filter changes what the first filter’s metrics can tell you. Section 01 The Second Filter There used to be one filter between your content and a human reader: the algorithm that decided whether to surface it. SEO was the science of surviving that filter. Understand what the algorithm rewarded, produce that, get shown. The optimization loop was legible: write for the machine so the machine shows you to the person. That loop still exists. But there's a second filter now sitting between the first one and the human, and it doesn't work the same way. The first filter decides what to surface. The second filter, the agent browsing on someone's behalf, decides what to read, what to summarize, what to pass along, and what to discard. Two machines in sequence before a person sees anything. I think the two filters create different pressures: earning attention and surviving compression. That is a way of looking at the problem, not a description of every ranking system. A hook may bring someone to a piece without helping a summary carry its argument. If the claim, evidence, and conclusion are hard to find, there is more room for the intermediary to lose the point. You spent years learning to write for a machine that showed you to people. Now there's another machine that reads you instead of them. And the human using that agent doesn't know what was omitted. They got an answer. The gap between your piece and their understanding is invisible to everyone. Section 02 The User Who Doesn't Know The human who uses a search engine today is often running their query through an agent without knowing it. Google now answers many questions directly at the top of the page, before any links. An assistant can assemble an answer with source links that the person may never open. These aren't power users with autonomous setups. They're ordinary people doing ordinary searches, and an intermediary is reading on their behalf before the results arrive. An answer can satisfy a search without bringing a reader to the source. That possibility matters here; it does not establish a traffic trend for every publisher. To know what is happening on a particular site, I would separate human visits, crawler requests, referrals, and completed actions. The traffic still comes. The reader behind it arrives less often. That's what makes the optimization instinct so counterproductive. The natural response to declining reach is to optimize harder for the first filter: more SEO, sharper hooks, better headlines. But if the bottleneck has shifted to the second filter, that optimization is solving for the wrong machine. You're getting better at being surfaced by something that routes you to something else that decides you're not worth reading directly. Section 03 What the Second Filter Reads A summary can carry the main claim while losing the sequence of examples that made it convincing. That matters when the point depends on how a reader reaches a conclusion, not just on the conclusion itself. What doesn't compress: vibe, accumulation, the texture of thinking rather than content. The movement from question to observation to something you didn't see coming. That movement is what produces curiosity in a reader, the sense that there's more to find, that the person writing knows something you haven't gotten to yet. The agent reads it, extracts the conclusion, passes along something technically accurate and entirely flat. The essay becomes a bullet point. The argument becomes a sentence. The curiosity doesn't make it through. If you optimize for both filters at once, you end up writing something compressible and positionally consistent. That's a different kind of writing than the kind worth doing. The filter doesn't just change what gets read. It changes what gets built, if you let it. Section 04 Digging with the Wrong Tool The optimization instinct is hard to kill because it used to work, and because the feedback loop that would tell you it stopped working is broken. A total request count does not tell you how many people read a piece. Search impressions and visits answer different questions, and crawler traffic needs separate analysis. The metrics can keep rewarding changes that do not bring more readers to the original piece. Check the version of the work that actually reaches the reader. Measurement is catching up. Google announced dedicated generative AI performance reports in June 2026 . Those reports help identify exposure; they still do not tell me whether a reader understood the argument. The production side compounds this. The content being published is increasingly agentic itself, as argued in the previous essay in this series. An agent creates the piece. Another distributes it. A third, on the reader's side, summarizes it for a human who may or may not have asked for it. At some point in that chain, the question of what any of it means to a person becomes genuinely hard to locate. A production chain instructed to chase SEO checklists and engagement hooks may reproduce those priorities at every step. That is a risk in how the workflow is configured, not proof of what every model was trained to reward. Google’s own guidance says there is no special writing style required for its generative search features. Section 05 The Thing the Filter Can't Flatten There's a version of this that ends in paralysis: if the filters flatten everything, why write anything? But that logic only holds if surviving the filters is the point. The reach model made that feel obvious: you write to be found, being found means a human read you, optimize to be found. Distribution and readership were treated as the same thing. They weren't, even before agents. The second filter just made the gap between them impossible to ignore. What the filter can't flatten is the reason someone seeks the original. A summary can carry a claim. It can't carry the judgment that the person who made the claim is worth trusting. That trust, the sense that a particular voice has a particular relationship to a domain over time, doesn't compress. It accumulates in the person, not in the agent. On the structural shift from reach to indexing, and on the synthesis-without-citation problem: "The Last Human Impression" (diegodella.ar, 2026). "The agent may draw on your perspective to form its answer, and the human who receives that answer never knows you exist. There is no traffic. No referral. The economic model for being synthesized rather than cited is still genuinely unresolved." ✦ ❧ ✦ I want to write work that gives someone a reason to seek the original. diegodella.ar · Buenos Aires, 2026 Share After You Post · Reading Path 01 The Empty Room 02 The Proxy Self 03 Writing for the Filter 04 The Trust Collapse 05 Origin Gravity The Proxy Self The Trust Collapse

zmox.html.before: Framework Paper / Media Strategy & Transformation The Constitutive Arc Published February 20, 2026 · Updated September 14, 2026 · by Diego Dell'Agostino The Constitutive Arc: a proposal for designing and assessing what readers learn through repeated contact with a source. Six Movements ~11,500 Words Diego Dell'Agostino ZMOT → Google · 2011 · Before purchase ZMOI → Dell'Agostino · Before belief CAX → Dell'Agostino · Before identity ZMOT ZMOI CAX CONSTITUTIVE ARC I Movement One The Collapse II Movement Two The Field III Movement Three The Ancestor IV Movement Four The Architecture V Movement Five The Danger VI Movement Six The Return ○ Movement I / Six The Collapse Around 1830–32, Katsushika Hokusai designed Under the Wave off Kanagawa , a woodblock print. Not when it broke. The moment before. White foam clawing upward, fishing boats reduced to splinters beneath it, the whole world contracted into a single instant of maximum tension. And there in the background, perfectly still, apparently small: Mount Fuji. Permanent. Indifferent. Present in a completely different register of time. Most people remember the wave. Almost nobody notices that the wave is the temporary thing. That is the problem this essay is about. ◆ ◆ ◆ Every media organization operating today is inside the wave. The fragmentation of attention, the collapse of direct traffic, algorithmic distribution, generative AI: real, immediate, violent. The rowers are right to hold on. What they cannot afford is to mistake the wave for the structure of the world. Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji shows a recurring subject from different places and under different conditions. I use that series as an image for a media source with a recognizable perspective across many encounters. That is my reading of the work, not a claim about Hokusai’s design intentions. We will return to that. ◆ ◆ ◆ The industry's diagnosis of its own crisis has been technically accurate and strategically useless. Attention fragmented: true. Trust in institutions eroded: true. Audiences now form opinions through feeds and messaging apps that no editorial team designed: true. All of it true. None of it the actual problem. The actual problem is that the industry has been measuring the wave and ignoring the mountain. Twenty years of optimizing for reach, engagement, time-on-platform (all measurements of the wave's surface) while the deeper structure beneath, the one that determines whether a media organization survives a disruption cycle, has been eroding without a metric attached to it. Lippmann saw it in 1922: the pictures in our heads are not formed from direct experience. They come from the narratives we consume, repeatedly, over time. McLuhan pushed further: the medium itself shapes cognitive structure, independent of content. What both were circling is this: the primary function of a media organization is not to distribute information. It is to participate in how its audience constructs reality. That function (constitutive rather than merely informational) is what has been lost. It is not a content problem. It is structural. I use “constitutive” to ask whether contact with a source contributes to how a reader understands a domain. That is a stronger claim than increasing time spent. It needs evidence of learning and independent judgment; the existence of a coherent publication does not establish it. Pillar I Infrastructure Production & Distribution Pillar II Legitimacy Institutional Authority Pillar III Narrative The Rebuilable Pillar Dalio's three pillars of dominant order applied to media. I and II are lost. III is the only one that can be rebuilt. The medium that loses narrative authority does not merely lose audience share. It loses its constitutive function: the ability to be part of how people build their understanding of reality. ◆ ◆ ◆ Ray Dalio maps how dominant orders rise and fall. The scale is empires and currencies, but the mechanism transfers. Dominant orders don't fall from frontal attack. They fall when an emergent force creates new terrain where the old order's advantages are irrelevant, captures the distribution layer, and by the time the incumbent notices, the perimeter has already moved. Three pillars hold a dominant order. Control of productive resources. Institutional legitimacy (the social agreement that this order is the right one). And narrative superiority: the capacity to define how reality gets interpreted. When all three align, the order is self-reinforcing. When two crack, the third cannot hold alone. Pre-digital media held all three. The infrastructure was capital-intensive, physically scarce, legally licensed. Owning a printing press or a broadcast license was not a content advantage; it was a structural barrier that made content advantages permanent. Legitimacy was codified: the press as the fourth estate, the byline as a credential. Narrative superiority was the automatic consequence of the other two. The platforms never attacked this directly. They had no interest in journalism. They built adjacent infrastructure (social connection, search, video) and in doing so quietly took the first pillar. Distribution. The trade routes. Once the routes changed hands, legitimacy began to shake, because legitimacy without reach is philosophy, not power. And when legitimacy shook, narrative authority drifted. When it drifted, it went somewhere. Authority is not destroyed. It migrates. Pre-2005 Editorial Holds all 3 pillars 2005–2012 Search & Social Capture distribution 2012–2019 Algorithmic Feed Capture interpretation 2020–now Generative AI Captures transformation ? Each phase appropriates the layer above. Authority does not disappear - it reconstitutes under new management. ◆ ◆ ◆ The Facebook feed of 2012 was not a neutral surface. It had editorial logic. It promoted content that generated emotional reaction. It suppressed content that generated reflection. Over hundreds of millions of daily interactions, it was building something: a version of reality organized around outrage, affiliation, and the compulsive need to know what happened next. Not by intention. By optimization. TikTok's For You Page is more precise and more consequential. It doesn't recommend content. It learns, at the individual level, the exact emotional frequencies that keep a specific person watching. It constructs for each user a personalized narrative environment calibrated to their particular vulnerabilities, curiosities, and desires. It is, in the most literal sense, a transformation engine. Not because anyone designed the transformation. Because that is what you get when you optimize for watch time at scale. The reader may not have chosen the sequence explicitly. The mechanism is visible now. When Facebook restructured its News Feed algorithm in 2012 to prioritize social engagement over chronological publishing, every publisher with distribution dependency on the platform lost a portion of narrative authority in a single policy change, with no input, no recourse. The authority migrated to the algorithm. The algorithm's editorial values became the de facto editorial values of every publisher whose reach ran through the feed. Publishers who recognized this built alternative distribution. Publishers who didn't found themselves a decade later producing content that satisfied the algorithm's values, because the algorithm was the only path to reach. The transformation of their audience was being designed daily by a system whose objectives were never disclosed. The TikTok FYP completed what the Facebook feed began. Where Facebook at least nominally connected users to sources they'd chosen to follow, the FYP eliminated the source relationship entirely. The user doesn't follow The Atlantic or The Guardian or The Economist. The user follows the FYP, which decides what those publications mean to that user: which pieces they see, in what sequence, next to what other content. The lens through which any piece of journalism reaches a reader is not the publication's lens. It's the FYP's lens. The constitutive function is captured upstream before the reader even arrives. ZMOT explained how brands win before purchase. ZMOI explained how media brands win before belief. The Constitutive Arc asks the question that follows: what happens to the audience after belief, and who designed that transformation? On the genealogy: ZMOT was built on behavioral data from thousands of buyers: empirical, measurable, falsifiable. ZMOI and the Constitutive Arc are prescriptive (built on argument, not measurement). The genealogy is conceptual, not evidential. That distinction should be declared rather than obscured. What follows is a claim about how media organizations should be built, not a report on how they behave. ◆ ◆ ◆ Generative AI does not add a new problem. It reveals the depth of the existing one. In the broadcast era, the transformation arc (the sequence of information, interpretation, and meaning a person consumed over time) was designed by editors. Someone had a point of view. The author existed. In the algorithmic era, the arc was generated by optimization functions. The author became a system. Transformation still occurred, but as byproduct rather than intention. In the AI era, something different happens: the arc emerges from the interaction itself. The user is not consuming a narrative someone else made. They are participating in the real-time generation of a narrative that has never existed before. Every AI conversation, every hyperpersonalized feed, every recommendation engine that has learned the specific shape of your cognition: these are not distribution systems. They are co-authorship systems. They produce transformation arcs that are, in the strictest sense, unique to each individual. Which means every media organization operating in an AI-mediated environment is producing personalized transformation arcs for its audience, whether it designed them or not. The arc exists. It occurs. The user experiences it and is changed. The only question is authorship. Did you design the transformation your system is producing? Or did you outsource it to a system optimizing for something else? If you haven't designed it, you haven't abdicated it. You've outsourced it. And the entity you outsourced it to has objectives that are not yours, and an audience relationship accountable to no values but its own. A media organization that does not intentionally design the transformation arc of its audience is not neutral. It is a passive conduit for transformations designed by other systems, toward other ends. ◆ ◆ ◆ Hokusai made thirty-six views of Fuji. Not because he was uncertain which was correct. Because he understood that a mountain can only be fully known through accumulated perspectives. Each one partial, each one true, the totality revealing something no single view could contain. He also understood something about the observer. The people in those boats, if they survive, are not the same people who left shore. The encounter with something vast and indifferent does something to the way you understand your own position. That is what a media organization can do at its highest. Not inform. Not entertain. Not even persuade. Give the audience a Fuji: something permanent, something that holds its shape across surfaces and crises. Show it from enough angles, with enough consistency, that the audience learns to see it themselves. Not to need you to see it. To have learned, through repeated encounter with your lens, a way of seeing that is now partly theirs. That is the function that was lost. That is what the wave obscured. That is what this essay proposes to rebuild. Not as nostalgia. As the only architecture that makes sense when the wave has passed and you need to know what is permanent. The wave is not the thing to understand. It never was. Coming next Movement II — The Field → ○○ Movement II / Six The Field Before naming the architecture, we need to name what changed. Not the technology. Something more foundational: the shape of the relationship between a media organization and the person it is trying to reach. For most of mass media history, that relationship had a geometry. Linear. A source emitted. A receiver consumed. The message traveled in one direction, arrived more or less intact, and the receiver was changed in ways the source could anticipate and design for. The broadcast model was not just technical architecture. It was a theory of transformation: the author shapes the arc, the audience walks it. That geometry is gone. Not disrupted. Gone. What replaced it doesn't have a clean name yet, which is partly why the industry keeps solving a geometric problem with linear tools and wondering why nothing works. What replaced it is a field. ◆ ◆ ◆ In physics, a field is not an object. It is a region of space where every point has a value: a potential, a force, a direction. It doesn't push you along a predetermined path. It structures the conditions under which any path you choose will unfold. Walk north, south, east, or west through a gravitational field: the field is present everywhere, shaping the cost and consequence of every step, without dictating which step you take. The empirical anchor: Melanie Green and Timothy Brock's Narrative Transportation Theory (2000) demonstrated that deep engagement with a narrative produces measurable belief change through "transportation"—absorption into the story world that reduces counter-argumentation. Subsequent research confirmed these effects compound across repeated exposure and are more durable than attitude change from direct argument. The field model is a design framework for producing transportation conditions intentionally, across multiple surfaces, over time. I am using that research to propose a design model. The model still needs testing. The organization no longer designs a path. It designs a field. Every user who enters walks their own version of it, shaped by their history, their attention, their entry point, their emotional state when they arrive. The path is unique. The field is shared. Most media strategy hasn't absorbed this. It still designs content as if there's a sequence the audience follows. Measures success as if there's a single arc to optimize. Treats editorial voice as if consistent tone from the source produces consistent experience for the receiver. None of these assumptions survive the field. The organization no longer designs a path. It designs a field. Every user walks their own version of it. The path is unique. The field is shared. The Path Model Linear. One arc. One direction. Start End All users → same sequence The Field Model Radial. Multiple arcs. One center. Lens Telegram Article Podcast Newsletter Video Push In the field model, each surface is a different angle of incidence into the same gravitational center. ◆ ◆ ◆ What does it mean to design a field rather than a path? The unit of design is no longer the article, the episode, the newsletter, or the post. Those are artifacts. The unit of design is the condition of encounter: the set of forces present regardless of which artifact the user picks up, which surface they enter from, where in their own arc they happen to be. A well-designed field has three properties a well-designed path doesn't need, because in a path they're given by the sequence. The first is coherence under variation. In a path, coherence is enforced by sequence. In a field, the user enters from any direction, at any point, in any order. Coherence can't be structural. It must be gravitational: something at the center of the field that pulls every encounter toward the same orientation, regardless of entry point. That center is the editorial lens. Not tone, not format, not platform. The lens: the specific, differentiated way the organization sees the world and makes that seeing contagious. The second is directionality without determinism. The organization can't control which path the user takes, but it can design the field so that all paths share a direction, so that wherever users enter and however they move, they tend to emerge with more understanding than they arrived with. The field exerts a force. It doesn't prescribe a destination. The third is transformation that compounds. In a path, transformation happens at the end. In a field, it's incremental and nonlinear. Each encounter adds a small charge. The charge accumulates across surfaces and time. What looks like a series of isolated contacts is a single extended process of constitution: the user becoming, gradually and through repetition, someone who sees the world through a lens they didn't have before. Coherence under variation. Directionality without determinism. Transformation that compounds. These are not content principles. They are field properties. They require a completely different kind of design. ◆ ◆ ◆ The field model changes the answer to almost every strategic question. Publishing cadence: in the path model, it's about maintaining momentum along a sequence. In the field model, it's about charge density: how frequently the user encounters the field, across how many surfaces, with what consistency of gravitational pull. Not how often you publish. How reliably the field is present in the user's day. Platform strategy: in the path model, platforms distribute the same sequence. In the field model, each surface is a different angle of incidence into the same field. The Telegram message is the field encountered at close range, high trust, low commitment. The long-form analysis is the field at depth, with time, in a receptive state. The browser notification is the field arriving unannounced at the moment of maximum interpretive openness. Different surfaces. Same field. Different depths of the same well. Completion tells you whether someone reached the end. CAX also asks whether their understanding changes over repeated encounters. That requires research with readers: what can they now explain, question, or investigate that they could not before? Retention and revenue still matter to the organization, but they do not substitute for evidence of learning. ◆ ◆ ◆ There is an objection practitioners raise first, and it contains a real tension. If every user designs their own path through the field, the organization loses the ability to construct shared experience. And without shared experience, there is no community; only a large number of individual users having individual encounters with artifacts that happen to share a brand. The objection is correct that the tension exists. It is wrong that the tension is fatal. Two people who walk different paths through the same gravitational field don't arrive at the same place. But they share something more durable than a common destination: a common orientation. They've been shaped by the same forces. They've developed, through their individual encounters with the field, a compatible way of seeing. That compatibility is the foundation of community—not identical content consumed simultaneously, but a shared lens through which different content is encountered and understood. This is a stronger foundation than broadcast ever provided. In the broadcast model, shared experience is synchronized but shallow. Everyone consumed the same news at the same time, but the transformation was minimal because the path was walked passively. In the field model, experience is asynchronous and individual, but transformation is deeper because the user navigates actively, encounters the lens from multiple angles, develops a relationship with it that is genuinely theirs. The community that emerges is not one of simultaneous consumption. It is one of constituted identity. The community the field produces is not one of simultaneous consumption. It is one of constituted identity: people who see the world compatibly because they were shaped by the same field, each in their own time, each through their own door. ◆ ◆ ◆ The field model has a practitioner's question attached to it. This question is the diagnostic that separates organizations thinking in field terms from those that aren't. Not: what is our content strategy? If a user encountered our field from ten different entry points, in ten different emotional states, on ten different surfaces, over six months—what would be the consistent force they felt pulling them in the same direction every time? If you can answer that with precision, you have a field. If the answer changes depending on the surface, the format, or who wrote the piece that day, you have a content operation. Content operations are not worthless. But they cannot produce the Constitutive Arc. Only fields can. A field is not a metaphor if it can be falsified. The following three proxies are the empirical floor: the minimum instrumentation required to distinguish a field from a content operation with aspirational language. Three falsifiable proxies - how to know if a field exists Proxy I Lens Consistency Test 5 pieces, 5 surfaces, same week. Ask 10 readers to identify the point of view. >70% agreement = field. <40% = content op. What it measures: Coherence under variation Proxy II Vocabulary Transfer Survey Survey at 3, 6, 12 months: "Describe how you think about [domain] in your own words." Code lens terms. Growth = lens transfer. Plateau = arc capture. What it measures: Transformation over time Proxy III - Critical Independence Reasoning Test Ask users to articulate two positions that disagree with the field, on a scale of 1–5. Cannot do it = capture. Does it = elixir. What it measures: Education vs. propaganda An organization that cannot pass Proxy I does not have a field. One that fails Proxy III has crossed into capture. The arc is not a path someone walks. It is a field someone is changed by. Coming next Movement III — The Ancestor → ○○○ Movement III / Six The Ancestor Nothing in this essay is new in the sense that matters most. The field model, the constitutive function, the idea that an audience is not a recipient of information but a traveler through a structured experience that changes who they are. None of this was invented by media strategy or by artificial intelligence or by the disruption cycle of the last twenty years. It was named, with extraordinary precision, more than seventy years ago by a man who was not thinking about media at all. Joseph Campbell published The Hero with a Thousand Faces in 1949. His subject was mythology. His method was comparative: he read the sacred stories of hundreds of cultures, across centuries and continents, and found beneath their surface differences a single deep structure that repeated with uncanny consistency. He called it the monomyth. Others called it the Hero's Journey. The names are less important than what he found. What he found was this: across every culture that Campbell surveyed (and the selection has been disputed by folklorists and anthropologists who argue he chose examples to confirm a structure already in mind) the stories that survive tend to share the same underlying architecture. A person begins in a known world. Something calls them beyond its borders. They cross a threshold into unfamiliar territory. They encounter trials, allies, and enemies. They find something they could not have found without leaving. They bring it back. And they return changed, not to the same world they left, but to a world that looks the same and is fundamentally different because they are. Note on Campbell: The academic critique of his universalism is legitimate: he selected his examples, and the monomyth is abstract enough to map onto almost any narrative if applied loosely. The Constitutive Arc uses the monomyth not as anthropological fact but as an operational heuristic for thinking about transformation arcs. Its value here is practical, not ethnographic. If a better structural model for designed transformation exists, the framework should use that instead. I use Campbell’s monomyth here as a way to describe change over time. ◆ ◆ ◆ Dan Harmon, the television writer, spent years trying to understand why certain stories work on audiences at a level that cannot be explained by craft alone. He arrived, independently, at Campbell. And then he did something Campbell had not done: he operationalized it. He compressed the monomyth into eight positions arranged in a circle, a tool that writers could use not just to analyze stories that already existed but to build new ones with the same deep structure. The eight positions are: you are in a zone of comfort, you want something, you enter an unfamiliar situation, you adapt to it, you get what you wanted, you pay a heavy price for it, you return to your familiar situation, you have changed. The circle is not a sequence of scenes. It is a map of transformation. It describes not what happens in a story but what has to happen inside the protagonist for the story to feel true. Credit belongs where it is due. Harmon's circle is a distillation of Campbell. Campbell's monomyth is a distillation of ten thousand years of human storytelling. The Constitutive Arc is built on both, and it would be intellectually dishonest to pretend otherwise. What this essay adds is not the discovery of the structure. It is the recognition that this structure is not only a property of fictional narratives. It is the structure of any genuine transformation, including the transformation that a media organization can produce in its audience over time, across surfaces, through intentional field design. ◆ ◆ ◆ The translation is not metaphorical. It is structural. Shared forward. Campbell's Monomyth mapped to the Constitutive Arc In the monomyth, the hero begins in the ordinary world: a place of comfort, familiarity, and incomplete understanding. In the Constitutive Arc, the ordinary world is the user before they encounter the field: existing frameworks inherited from prior sources, experience, ambient culture. Those frameworks are functional. They are also the starting condition: the state the field will gradually expand, complicate, and ultimately replace with something more sophisticated. The call to adventure is the disruption that makes the ordinary world untenable. In the Constitutive Arc, the call is the first genuine contact with the field: the piece that reframes something the user thought they understood, the analysis that introduces a vocabulary they did not have, the argument that reveals a pattern they had been living inside without being able to name. The call is the moment the field makes itself felt as something other than ambient information. It exerts a pull. The crossing of the threshold corresponds to the user's shift from casual contact to habitual engagement. They begin to return. They bring questions to the field rather than waiting for the field to raise questions for them. They are no longer passively receiving content. They are actively navigating the field, which means the field is beginning to shape not just what they know but how they think. The road of trials is the extended middle: the accumulation of encounters across surfaces and time that gradually displace old frameworks with new ones. It is not dramatic. It does not announce itself. It is the slow, compound work of a field that is coherent enough, present enough, and differentiated enough to keep exerting its gravitational pull through months of ordinary contact. The innermost cave (where the hero confronts the thing they have been most afraid of) corresponds in the Constitutive Arc to the moment of genuine cognitive displacement. The user arrives at a point where the field has given them enough of a new lens that they can see something they could not see before, and that seeing requires them to let go of a prior certainty. This is transformation at its most real and most uncomfortable. It is also the moment the field earns its constitutive status: not because it delivered information, but because it changed the structure through which information is processed. The return with the elixir (the hero coming back carrying something that did not exist in the ordinary world) is the user who shares, who references, who explains to someone else a way of seeing they did not have before they entered the field. They have become a distribution node not because they were incentivized to share but because the transformation they experienced is genuinely valuable and they know it. The elixir is not a piece of content. It is a lens. And lenses, unlike articles, replicate themselves through conversation. The elixir the user carries back is not a piece of content. It is a lens. And lenses, unlike articles, replicate themselves through conversation. ◆ ◆ ◆ The reason this mapping matters is not that it gives media strategists a new way to think about editorial arcs for individual pieces. It matters because it reveals what the field needs to be at a structural level in order to produce genuine transformation rather than mere engagement. A field that only provides the ordinary world (comfort, confirmation, familiar frameworks restated with new data) cannot produce the Constitutive Arc. It produces loyalty without growth, which is another name for dependency. A field that only provides trials (constant disruption, relentless challenge, no stable ground) cannot produce the Constitutive Arc either. It produces anxiety without orientation, which is another name for churn. The field that produces the Constitutive Arc provides both: a stable enough center that the user can orient themselves, and a consistent enough pull toward the unfamiliar that they keep moving. The center is the lens. The pull is the editorial ambition. The arc is what happens to the user when both are present over time. Campbell spent years asking why certain stories survive across thousands of years and others disappear. His answer was that the stories that survive tend to be the ones that map most accurately onto the structure of human transformation—or, more carefully: the stories that survive are the ones we have selected across generations precisely because they feel true, and what feels true about them is a real process: the process by which a person becomes capable of something they were not capable of before. Whether survival caused the structure or the structure caused survival is a question Campbell could not resolve. What remains useful is the structure itself. The proposed arc uses a narrative model to plan how readers might develop their understanding over time. Use it to choose examples, introduce disagreements, and offer a next step. Then check whether readers find those choices useful. The audience is not a market to capture. It is a collection of people who are, whether they name it or not, in the middle of their own journeys. The field that understands this, that positions itself not as a source of information but as a companion to the transformation already underway—is the field that becomes constitutive. It becomes part of the journey itself, not a service consumed along the way. The oldest stories knew what the newest media strategies are only beginning to relearn: transformation is the product. Everything else is the packaging. Coming next Movement IV — The Architecture → ○○○○ Movement IV / Six The Architecture The Constitutive Arc is not only a theory of what media organizations should aspire to. It is a practical claim about how they should be built. Which means it needs an architectural language: a way of looking at the existing components of a media business and asking, for each one, not what function it serves internally, but what role it plays in the user's transformation. The most widely used framework for mapping a business's components is the Business Model Canvas, developed by Alexander Osterwalder. It organizes a business into nine building blocks: customer segments, value proposition, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships, and cost structure. It is a tool for understanding what a business does and how it sustains itself. It is not a tool for understanding what a business does to the people it serves. The Constitutive Arc proposes a rearticulation. Not a replacement. The Canvas remains useful for operational planning. But when you lay the monomyth's structure over the Canvas's nine blocks, something becomes visible that was not visible before: every block has not only an operational function but a narrative function. Every element of the business is either serving the user's transformation or it is not. And if it is not, it is not neutral; it is actively working against the field's coherence. A note on prior frameworks: Jobs To Be Done asks what the user hires a product to do in their life. Brand Purpose asks what the organization does in the world beyond its output. Both are genuine advances over feature-based value propositions, and both share the constitutive intuition that output is not the product. The Constitutive Arc builds on both and adds a dimension neither addresses directly: it asks at which stage of the transformation arc the user is when they hire for that job, and how that stage changes what the field owes them. A first-contact user in the ordinary world needs a different encounter than a user past the innermost cave carrying a new lens. JTBD segments by job. Brand Purpose declares the mission. CAX segments by arc position and designs the encounter accordingly. That is not the same question, and it requires different instrumentation. The Constitutive Arc does not arrive in a vacuum. The last twenty years have produced a serious literature on how media organizations create value that goes beyond content delivery. Each framework in that literature solved a real problem and created a blind spot. Understanding where CAX sits relative to that landscape is not a footnote; it is the argument for why a new framework is needed at all. McKinsey's Consumer Decision Journey (2009) was the first significant post-funnel framework in marketing: it replaced the linear AIDA model with a loyalty loop that acknowledged ongoing relationship. It was correct in its diagnosis and limited in its prescription: the loop describes behavior, not design. It tells organizations that consumers return. It does not tell them what to build so that returning deepens rather than merely repeats. Ben Thompson’s Aggregation Theory examines how platforms gain power through their relationship with users and suppliers. CAX asks a different practical question for publishers: what makes sustained contact with a source worthwhile to a reader? An identifiable editorial perspective is my proposed answer, but the framework still has to show that it improves understanding and supports return. The Content Marketing Flywheel (popularized by HubSpot and now standard terminology) argues that content creates attraction, which creates engagement, which creates sales, which creates more content through customer advocacy. It is correct about the loop. It is silent on what determines whether the loop deepens or merely repeats. A flywheel generates momentum. It does not generate transformation. Audiences can spin in a flywheel for years without being substantively changed by the content they consume. The Constitutive Arc asks what happens inside the loop: whether the repetition is producing accumulation or just traffic. The Attention Economy framework (Herbert Simon's scarcity diagnosis, Tim Wu's operationalization) correctly identifies that attention is the resource media organizations compete for. But attention as the unit of value produces a specific design pressure: maximize time spent, minimize friction, optimize for return. None of these pressures are oriented toward transformation. A user who spends four hours a day with a field and leaves unchanged has not experienced the Constitutive Arc; they have experienced arc capture, one of the failure modes in Movement V. The Attention Economy is the problem diagnosis. The Constitutive Arc is a proposed answer to the question the Attention Economy never asks: attention toward what end? Customer segments in the conventional Canvas are defined by demographics, behavior, or need. In the Constitutive Arc, they are defined by arc position. Where is the user in their journey? Are they in the ordinary world, not yet aware the field exists? Are they at the threshold, returning occasionally but not yet committed? Are they in the road of trials, actively navigating the field across multiple surfaces? Are they past the innermost cave, already carrying a new lens and ready to share it? Segmenting by demographics tells you who is in the room. Segmenting by arc position tells you where they are in the journey, which is the only segmentation that determines what the field should do next. Channels in the conventional Canvas are distribution mechanisms. In the Constitutive Arc, every channel is a threshold: a specific mode of entry into the field, each with its own attention state, trust level, and depth of engagement. A browser extension or new tab is ambient presence: the field arriving at the moment of maximum cognitive openness, before the day's noise has accumulated. A Telegram message is high-trust, close-range contact: the field arriving as a companion rather than a publisher. A long-form analysis is the field at depth: the user has chosen to go further, which means they are already past the threshold and ready for trial-level encounter. Designing channels as thresholds means asking, for each surface: what arc stage is the user typically at when they encounter us here, and is this encounter designed for that stage? The value proposition is where the rearticulation is most radical. In the conventional Canvas, the value proposition answers: what problem do we solve, and why are we better than the alternative? In the Constitutive Arc, the value proposition answers a different question entirely: what does the user become, through sustained contact with this field, that they could not become without it? The output (the articles, the analyses, the videos) is not the value proposition. It is the delivery mechanism. The value proposition is the transformation the field makes possible. And if the organization cannot state that transformation with precision, it does not yet have a constitutive value proposition. It has a content library. Customer relationships in the conventional Canvas range from automated to personal. In the Constitutive Arc, the relationship has a specific character that neither pole captures: it is companionship through the journey. The ally in the monomyth is not a service provider. The ally is someone who has walked a similar road and offers the traveler something specific to their current position: a warning before the cave, a tool for crossing the threshold, recognition of what was gained in the return. A media organization that designs its relationship model as companionship, that asks, at each touchpoint, what does a traveler at this stage of the arc need from a trusted companion right now—is designing something categorically different from engagement optimization. Key resources in the conventional Canvas are the assets required to deliver the value proposition. In the Constitutive Arc, the primary key resource is the lens itself. Not the technology stack, not the distribution infrastructure, not the talent pool, though all of these matter. The lens: the organization's specific, differentiated, intellectually honest way of seeing the domain it covers. The lens is the gravitational center of the field. Everything else in the business (every channel, every relationship, every content format) is a delivery mechanism for the lens. An organization that loses its lens has not lost a competitive advantage. It has lost the field. It becomes, at that point, a content operation with good distribution. The lens is the perspective a reader learns to recognize across the work. It includes the questions the source asks and the evidence it takes seriously. CAX proposes that repeated contact with that perspective can help readers develop their own understanding. That value needs to be demonstrated; it is not immune to imitation. ◆ ◆ ◆ The rearticulation of the Canvas through the Constitutive Arc produces one diagnostic question for each block.
